units.name: Meeting and Greeting
units.focus: Greetings, introductions, WH questions, subject pronouns, be and punctuation.

lessons.title: Greet and introduce yourself
lessons.outcome: Exchange a greeting and give a clear three-part introduction.
lessons.criteria: Match 4/5 greeting phrases; retrieve 3/4 listening facts; introduce name, hometown and study
lessons.vocab: greeting = words/actions used to say hello; introduce = tell someone your name; hometown = town you come from; study = learn a subject; polite = showing respect.
lessons.model: A: Good morning. My name is Ahmed. I am from Salalah. I study English. B: Nice to meet you. I am Lina. Practise I am / I'm.
lessons.ccq: Is Good morning suitable at 9 a.m. or 9 p.m.? 9 a.m. Do we say Nice to meet you when first introduced? Yes.
lessons.lead: Greet two learners formally and informally. Learners identify the difference and suggest familiar greeting words.
lessons.controlled: Match hello, good morning, goodbye, nice to meet you and thank you to the five meanings in the companion check.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U1-A in the input bank. First identify the purpose; then complete name, age, city and study. Compare answers.
lessons.task: New-classmate role-play: each learner greets, introduces three details and responds politely. Change partners and repeat without reading.
lessons.check: Match: hello / good morning / goodbye / nice to meet you / thank you. Meanings: 1 leave; 2 morning; 3 appreciation; 4 first introduction; 5 general greeting. U1-A: name, age, city, study?
lessons.answers: Matching: goodbye; good morning; thank you; nice to meet you; hello. U1-A: Huda; 18; Salalah; English. Purpose: introduce herself.
lessons.exitq: Write a suitable morning greeting and two sentences introducing yourself.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: suitable greeting. 1 point: two understandable personal-information sentences. Example: Good morning. I am Ali. I am from Salalah.
lessons.barrier: Learners repeat the greeting but cannot supply their own details.
lessons.support: Use a name/city/study card and rehearse with one partner before changing partners.
lessons.nextstep: Give a new identity card and check whether the learner can introduce it independently.
lessons.home: Practise a 20-second introduction; complete the sentence stems on p. 22 using chosen or fictional details.
lessons.prior: Basic spoken English and familiar college/workplace experiences; diagnose in the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Ask questions and read for meaning
lessons.outcome: Find key ideas about meeting people and ask appropriate introductory questions.
lessons.criteria: Answer 4/5 selected reading items; choose 4/5 question words; ask and answer three introductory questions
lessons.vocab: trust = belief that someone is honest; custom = usual practice in a community; respectful = showing consideration; who = asks about a person; where = asks about a place.
lessons.model: Where are you from? I am from Oman. Who is your teacher? Ms. Amina. When is your class? On Sunday. Stress the question word.
lessons.ccq: Does where ask about a person or a place? A place. Does why ask for a reason? Yes.
lessons.lead: Retrieve Sunday introductions. Ask which extra detail a new classmate could ask for.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 5; complete p. 6 A1-3 and B4-5. Underline a text clue for each answer. Discuss customs as examples, not rules for every person.
lessons.guided: Sort who/what/where/when/why by meaning; complete the five companion items. Use p. 15 C for matching if time permits.
lessons.task: Welcome-desk interview: ask three questions, record a partner's answers, then introduce the partner to a new pair.
lessons.check: Reading: p. 6 A1-3, B4-5. Complete: 1 ___ are you from? 2 ___ is your name? 3 ___ is your teacher? 4 ___ is your birthday? 5 ___ are you learning English?
lessons.answers: Reading: F, T, F; 4 c (United States); 5 b (bowing), according to the text. Question words: Where, What, Who, When, Why. p. 15 C: 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-e, 5-b.
lessons.exitq: Write a question for each answer: I am from Muscat. My name is Sara.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: Where are you from? What is your name? Accept equivalent correct questions.
lessons.barrier: Learners use what for every question.
lessons.support: Keep a person/place/time/reason chart visible during practice, then remove it for the exit.
lessons.nextstep: Use two new answers and ask learners to select and produce the matching question.
lessons.home: Complete p. 15 D; read the cultural greetings on pp. 8-11 as consolidation.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Use pronouns and the verb be
lessons.outcome: Introduce people with accurate subject pronouns and affirmative, negative and question forms of be.
lessons.criteria: Complete 4/5 pronoun/be items; form a negative and a question correctly; describe two people and check a detail
lessons.vocab: subject = person/thing the sentence is about; pronoun = word replacing a noun; affirmative = positive statement; negative = statement with not; contraction = shortened form.
lessons.model: This is Salim. He is a student. He is not a teacher. Is he from Salalah? Yes, he is. They are students. Practise is / isn't and are / aren't.
lessons.ccq: In They are students, is they one person or more than one here? More than one. Does Is he...? start with the verb? Yes.
lessons.lead: Show two names and one college object. Elicit he/she/they/it using fictional identity cards.
lessons.controlled: Complete the five companion pronoun/be items individually; compare with p. 16 and the be table on p. 20.
lessons.guided: Use p. 21 C1-3 and question task D1-3. Change sentences to negatives and questions; rehearse short answers in pairs.
lessons.task: Identity-card information gap: A describes two fictional students; B asks questions to identify the cards. Swap roles.
lessons.check: 1 Sara is a student. ___ is 18. 2 Ali and I: ___. 3 I ___ ready. 4 She ___ from Oman. 5 They ___ students. Change She is a teacher to negative; You are from Oman to a question.
lessons.answers: She; we; am; is; are. She is not/isn't a teacher. Are you from Oman? p. 21 C: I am not late; They are not busy; She is not a teacher. Questions: Are you from Oman? Is he a new student? Are they in the classroom?
lessons.exitq: Correct: He are a student. Change They are ready into a question.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: He is a student. Are they ready?
lessons.barrier: Learners omit be or use one form with every subject.
lessons.support: Use a three-column I-am / he-she-it-is / you-we-they-are chart and movable word cards.
lessons.nextstep: Ask for one fresh sentence and question using we, with the chart hidden.
lessons.home: Complete p. 16 C and write the three- or four-sentence introduction on p. 17.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Read greetings and punctuate a dialogue
lessons.focus: Cultural reading, punctuation and everyday English
lessons.outcome: Recognise greeting customs in a text and write a clearly punctuated short café exchange.
lessons.criteria: Identify three text-based greeting examples; correct 4/5 punctuation features; perform a four-turn café exchange
lessons.vocab: culture = shared practices and ideas; tradition = practice passed on over time; capital = large letter; apostrophe = mark for missing letters or possession; full stop = statement-ending mark.
lessons.model: A: Good morning. Can I have tea, please? B: Certainly. A: How much is it? B: It is one rial. Example price is fictional.
lessons.ccq: Does Can I have tea end with a full stop or a question mark? A question mark. Which letter is always capital in I'm? I.
lessons.lead: Compare hello, goodbye and good morning; learners choose a suitable phrase for a café customer.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 9 and locate the greetings linked to Japan, New Zealand and the UK. Share one supporting phrase for each.
lessons.guided: Use pp. 18-19 to edit the companion dialogue. Then listen to U1-B and note the item and price.
lessons.task: Use the fictional menu in the input bank. In pairs, write and perform a four-turn order with greeting, request, price question and polite response.
lessons.check: Text: greetings linked to Japan, New Zealand, UK? Edit: good morning im ali can i have tea please. U1-B: drink and price?
lessons.answers: Text: bowing; hongi; formal handshake/How do you do and informal greetings. Edited: Good morning. I'm Ali. Can I have tea, please? Check capital G/I/A, apostrophe, full stops, question mark, comma. U1-B: tea; one rial.
lessons.exitq: Punctuate: im huda. Then write a polite question asking for water.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: I'm Huda. 1 point: Can/Could I have water, please? or another accurate polite question.
lessons.barrier: Learners know punctuation names but do not apply them in writing.
lessons.support: Colour-code sentence starts and endings; edit one shared example before independent work.
lessons.nextstep: Give a new two-line dialogue and check capitals, apostrophe and sentence endings.
lessons.home: Complete selected p. 19 punctuation tasks; rehearse your café dialogue.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Welcome a new classmate
lessons.outcome: Write a short introduction and conduct a polite meeting with a new classmate.
lessons.criteria: Edit four language/punctuation features; plan four relevant details; produce 5-6 clear sentences and a short exchange
lessons.vocab: detail = a specific piece of information; draft = first version; revise = improve the message; edit = correct language; response = an answer.
lessons.model: Hello. My name is Lina. I am from Salalah. I am a vocational college student. This is my friend Noor. She is friendly. We study English together.
lessons.ccq: Does We include only my friend? No, it includes my friend and me. Does a question need an answer in the dialogue? Yes.
lessons.lead: Retrieve one greeting, one WH question and one be sentence without notes.
lessons.controlled: Correct the four companion errors. Identify where the unit model uses I, she and we.
lessons.guided: Use p. 22 stems to plan name, hometown, study and interest. Rehearse the ideas with a partner; add a friend using a pronoun.
lessons.task: Write 5-6 introduction sentences, then act out the p. 23 meeting with two questions each. Assess the writing and each learner's contribution using the unit rubric.
lessons.check: Correct: 1 i am salim. 2 She are my friend. 3 Where you are from? 4 Im a student.
lessons.answers: I am Salim. She is my friend. Where are you from? I'm a student. Accept I am a student. Look for original details rather than copying the model.
lessons.exitq: Write one accurate question for a new classmate and one corrected sentence from your draft.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for an accurate, relevant question; 1 point for a corrected sentence. Record the full performance separately out of 10.
lessons.barrier: Learners copy a model without changing its details.
lessons.support: Give a four-box plan; cover the model during drafting and allow fictional details.
lessons.nextstep: Start Unit 2 by reteaching the most frequent be or punctuation error using a new occupation sentence.
lessons.home: Submit a clean introduction and highlight one change made after feedback.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

inputs: U1-A | A new student | Sunday
Good morning. My name is Huda. I am eighteen years old. I am from Salalah. I study English at a vocational college. I like reading and drawing. I am happy to meet my new classmates.
Questions: What is the purpose? Record name, age, city and study.
Key: introduction; Huda; 18; Salalah; English.
U1-B | In a cafe | Wednesday
Server: Good morning. Can I help you? Customer: Yes, can I have tea, please? Server: Certainly. Customer: How much is it? Server: It is one rial. Customer: Thank you. Server: You are welcome.
Questions: What does the customer order? How much is it? Which phrase makes the request polite?
Key: tea; one rial; please / Can I have...?. Fictional price.
card: FICTIONAL ROLE CARDS AND MENU

Student A: Ali, from Sohar, studies English. Student B: Noor, from Salalah, studies English. First meet, then introduce the other student. Cafe menu: tea 1 rial; water 0.5 rial; sandwich 1.5 rials. Ask for an item and check the price. These are classroom prices.
extra: I am / you are / he is / she is / it is / we are / they are. For a question, move be before the subject: Are you a student? For a negative, add not: She is not a teacher. Use capitals for I, names and sentence starts; ? for direct questions; apostrophes in I'm and name's.
resources.model: Hello, my name is Lina. I am from Salalah. I am a vocational college student. This is my friend Noor. She is friendly. We study English together.
rubric: Greeting and at least three relevant details
Clear pronouns and accurate be forms
Five or six connected introduction sentences
Capitals, full stops, question marks and apostrophes
Polite exchange with questions and suitable responses
resources.quick: 1. Complete: I ___ a student. 2. ___ are you from? 3. Correct: She are my friend. 4. Punctuate: im ali.
resources.quickkey: 1 am; 2 Where; 3 She is my friend; 4 I'm Ali.
resources.feedback: Your introduction is clear. Check the verb after she, then correct one sentence and read it aloud.

units.name: Jobs and Traits
units.focus: Occupations, personal qualities, job advertisements, scanning and a/an/the.

lessons.title: Name occupations and match traits
lessons.outcome: Describe an occupation and explain one useful personal quality.
lessons.criteria: Match 5/6 jobs to functions; retrieve 3/4 listening details; describe a job with a relevant trait and reason
lessons.vocab: occupation = job; trait = personal quality; patient = able to wait calmly; reliable = can be trusted; creative = able to develop new ideas; skill = ability to do something.
lessons.model: A mechanic repairs cars. A mechanic should be careful because small mistakes can cause problems. She is an engineer. Stress en-gi-NEER.
lessons.ccq: Is patient a job or a quality? A quality. Does reliable mean we can trust the person? Yes.
lessons.lead: Learners name jobs they know and point to a picture on p. 42; accept a guess before teaching the English word.
lessons.controlled: Match the six jobs and functions on p. 42. Check by saying A nurse cares for sick people rather than only a letter.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U2-A about a technician. Record job, workplace and two traits; explain the evidence for each trait.
lessons.task: Job-clue game: describe duties, workplace and one trait without saying the job. Partner guesses and asks one question.
lessons.check: p. 42: pilot, architect, marine navigator, nurse, accountant, carpenter: functions? U2-A: job, workplace and two traits?
lessons.answers: Pilot-flies planes; architect-designs buildings; marine navigator-guides ships; nurse-cares for sick people; accountant-manages financial records; carpenter-builds/repairs wooden structures. U2-A: electronics technician; workshop; patient and cooperative.
lessons.exitq: Name one job, state one duty and give one suitable trait with a reason.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for an accurate job-duty pair; 1 point for a plausible trait with reason. Example: A teacher teaches students. A teacher is patient because learners need time.
lessons.barrier: Learners list adjectives without explaining how they relate to a job.
lessons.support: Use job / duty / trait / because columns and one worked example.
lessons.nextstep: Offer a different job and ask for a new trait-reason link.
lessons.home: Learn six job words; use p. 43 unscrambling as consolidation.
lessons.prior: Basic spoken English and familiar college/workplace experiences; diagnose in the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Read about people and their work
lessons.outcome: Retrieve and compare job, location and contribution details in two profiles.
lessons.criteria: Answer 4/4 true-false items; complete 3/4 profile details; compare two workers using text evidence
lessons.vocab: engineer = person who designs/builds technical systems; entrepreneur = person who starts a business; ministry = government department; eco-friendly = intended to reduce environmental harm; community = people in an area.
lessons.model: Shamis is an agricultural engineer. He works in Sohar. Lara is an entrepreneur. She makes eco-friendly bags. Both solve problems.
lessons.ccq: Did Shamis study in Saham or work there in this text? Study there. Does eco-friendly mean harmful to nature? No.
lessons.lead: Display engineer and entrepreneur. Learners predict one task for each before reading.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 30 and complete p. 31 C1-4. Correct false statements with evidence from the text.
lessons.guided: Complete p. 31 D1-4 and E1-4 in pairs. Underline the line that supports each answer.
lessons.task: Choose a guest for a college careers talk: Shamis or Lara. Present two text facts and explain why that person suits your class.
lessons.check: p. 31 C1-4, D1-4 and E1-4. Vocabulary p. 29 A: engineer, entrepreneur, ministry, eco-friendly.
lessons.answers: C: F,T,F,T. Shamis works in Sohar and has two children. D: Saham; German; food; team. E: Lara, Shamis, Lara, Shamis. Vocabulary: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b.
lessons.exitq: Write one accurate fact about Shamis and one about Lara without looking at the text.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for each accurate fact. Example: Shamis helps farmers. Lara lives in Berlin.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse the place of study with the place of work.
lessons.support: Use separate study/work/location boxes and highlight signal words.
lessons.nextstep: Read a short new profile and ask learners to separate study place from workplace.
lessons.home: Read Li Wei on p. 33; answer questions 4-7 and compare two of his jobs.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Scan a job advertisement and letters
lessons.outcome: Locate vacancy requirements and follow an application-to-interview sequence.
lessons.criteria: Find 4/4 advertisement facts; locate three application/interview details; explain the next step for an applicant
lessons.vocab: vacancy = available job; salary = pay for work; apply = ask formally for a job; resume/CV = record of qualifications and experience; interview = meeting to discuss suitability.
lessons.model: The vacancy is for a mechanic in Wadi Al Kabir. The salary in this textbook advertisement is 850 OMR. Hamdan is invited to an interview.
lessons.ccq: Does an interview invitation mean the applicant definitely has the job? No. Do we scan every word slowly? No; we look for a specific detail.
lessons.lead: Ask where students might see job information. Predict what an advertisement must tell an applicant.
lessons.controlled: Scan p. 37 for company type, location, work and salary. Set a short time limit; underline only the matching details.
lessons.guided: Read pp. 38-39: find when Hamdan can start, what he attaches, and the interview date/time. Distinguish the letter's real purpose from its heading.
lessons.task: Applicant/adviser role-play: explain the vacancy, required documents and interview arrangements using notes; answer a follow-up question.
lessons.check: p. 37 questions 1-4. pp. 38-39: start date; attachments; interview date/time; three items to bring?
lessons.answers: Mechanical maintenance company; Wadi Al Kabir; maintenance of air conditioners, lifts/elevators; 850 OMR (textbook example). Start immediately; CV/resume and two recent 2x2 photos; 10 September 2024 at 10 a.m.; ID card, college certificate and other certificates. The letter invites him to interview.
lessons.exitq: State the advertised salary and explain whether the p. 39 letter confirms employment or invites an interview.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: 850 OMR. 1 point: interview invitation, not confirmed employment. Treat all dates/pay as historical text details.
lessons.barrier: Learners assume the heading letter of acceptance means the job is confirmed.
lessons.support: Compare the verbs invite and employ; point to We want to invite you for an interview.
lessons.nextstep: Show a short invitation and an offer; ask learners to identify each purpose.
lessons.home: Finish the remaining p. 39 questions; make a three-step application checklist.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Use a, an and the in job descriptions
lessons.outcome: Use articles to introduce occupations and refer to a specific person or place.
lessons.criteria: Choose 4/5 articles correctly; explain a/an using the next sound; describe a job and identify a specific workplace
lessons.vocab: article = a, an or the before a noun; vowel sound = sound at the start of engineer; specific = clearly identified; uniform = clothing worn for a job; accountant = person who manages financial records.
lessons.model: She is an engineer. He is a university student. I know a mechanic. The mechanic works near my home. A/an depends on sound, not only spelling.
lessons.ccq: Do we say a uniform or an uniform? A uniform: it starts with a /y/ sound. Does the mechanic refer back to someone already introduced? Yes.
lessons.lead: Retrieve six job names. Learners say I want to be... and notice a or an before the job.
lessons.controlled: Complete the five companion article choices; explain two answers. Use the rule table on p. 40.
lessons.guided: Complete p. 41 conversation; in pairs make a new version about a different career and training place.
lessons.task: Careers adviser dialogue: learner describes a dream job, a workplace and a useful quality. Partner asks two questions; swap roles.
lessons.check: Choose articles: 1 ___ doctor; 2 ___ engineer; 3 ___ uniform; 4 I met a nurse. ___ nurse was friendly; 5 ___ accountant. p. 41 conversation blanks?
lessons.answers: a; an; a; The; an. p. 41: a chef; a good cooking school; an excellent school; the city centre. Accept centre/center spelling.
lessons.exitq: Complete: She is ___ electrician. I bought a uniform. ___ uniform is blue.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: an; The.
lessons.barrier: Learners choose a/an by written letters instead of sounds.
lessons.support: Say the next word aloud and sort engineer/doctor/uniform before adding the article.
lessons.nextstep: Check a university student and an office worker orally, then in writing.
lessons.home: Write three original article sentences from p. 41 and prepare notes for My Dream Job.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Present your dream job
lessons.outcome: Give a short career talk and write a connected job description with accurate articles.
lessons.criteria: Correct four job/article errors; plan duty, workplace and two traits; present and write 5-6 relevant sentences
lessons.vocab: responsibility = duty you must do; qualification = recognised evidence of study/training; ambition = strong aim; teamwork = working well with others; example = detail showing an idea.
lessons.model: I want to be an electrician. An electrician works with electrical systems. This job needs careful work and training. I am patient and I enjoy solving problems.
lessons.ccq: Is I am friendly a duty or a trait? A trait. Does because explain why a quality matters? Yes.
lessons.lead: Use rapid job clues from Sunday; invite learners to recall a useful quality for each job.
lessons.controlled: Correct the four companion examples, checking both meaning and articles.
lessons.guided: Use p. 44 questions to make a four-box plan: job/workplace/duties/traits. Partner asks for one missing detail.
lessons.task: Deliver a 45-60-second career talk and answer one question. Write 5-6 connected sentences; peer-check articles and reasons. Use the unit rubric.
lessons.check: Correct: 1 I want to be a engineer. 2 An carpenter builds furniture. 3 I need an uniform. 4 A nurse flies planes.
lessons.answers: an engineer; A carpenter; a uniform; A nurse cares for sick people (or A pilot flies planes). Accept another accurate duty.
lessons.exitq: Write one accurate job sentence and add a reason for a useful trait.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: accurate job sentence with article. 1 point: relevant trait-reason link. Score the full performance separately /10.
lessons.barrier: Learners memorise a job title but cannot explain duties or qualities.
lessons.support: Allow a keyword card; ask What do you do? Where? What quality helps? before drafting.
lessons.nextstep: Open Unit 3 with one revised occupation sentence linked to protective equipment.
lessons.home: Revise the job description and circle a, an and the; retain it in the writing portfolio.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

inputs: U2-A | An electronics technician | Sunday

My name is Salma. I am an electronics technician. I work in a workshop with a small team. I am patient because finding a fault can take time. I am cooperative because I listen to my colleagues and share ideas. I enjoy learning how electronic systems work.
Questions: What is her job? Where does she work? Which two traits does she explain?
Key: electronics technician; workshop; patient; cooperative.
card: JOB-CLUE CARDS

Pilot: flies planes. Architect: designs buildings. Marine navigator: guides ships. Nurse: cares for sick people. Accountant: manages financial records. Carpenter: builds and repairs wooden structures. Give a duty and workplace clue; partner names the job. Add a trait with a reason; accept different plausible traits.
extra: For the p. 37 historical advertisement, locate job/company/location/pay instead of reading every word slowly. The p. 39 letter is an interview invitation even though its heading says acceptance. A/an depends on the next sound: an engineer, a mechanic, a uniform, a university student. Use the for a person or item already identified.
resources.model: I want to be an electrician. An electrician works with electrical systems in buildings. This job needs careful work and proper training. I am patient because I enjoy solving difficult problems. I also like teamwork because colleagues can share useful ideas. I would like to work for a company that helps me develop my skills.
rubric: Accurate job, duties and workplace
Two relevant qualities with reasons
Appropriate a/an/the
Five or six connected sentences with clear punctuation
Short talk from notes and a relevant response
resources.quick: 1. ___ engineer. 2. ___ uniform. 3. A carpenter flies planes: correct the duty. 4. Does an interview invitation confirm employment?
resources.quickkey: 1 an; 2 a; 3 builds/repairs wooden structures; 4 no.
resources.feedback: You named the job and workplace. Add why one personal quality is useful in this job.

units.name: Safety and Precautions
units.focus: Protective equipment, signs, marine safety, requests, plurals and must/should.

lessons.title: Name clothing and protective equipment
lessons.outcome: Distinguish clothing types and link protective equipment to body parts.
lessons.criteria: Name 5/6 equipment items; match three clothing headings and retrieve 3/4 listening facts; explain three equipment/body-part links
lessons.vocab: protective = intended to reduce harm; casual = everyday, informal; formal = suitable for an official occasion; goggles = protective eyewear; boots = strong footwear; overalls = protective work clothing.
lessons.model: Goggles protect the eyes. Boots protect the feet. A helmet protects the head. Use the PPE approved for the specific task; ordinary clothing is not automatically protective.
lessons.ccq: Are goggles worn on the eyes or feet? Eyes. Does every glove protect against every hazard? No; selection depends on the task.
lessons.lead: Compare a normal shirt and pictures of work clothing on p. 47; elicit their names and purposes.
lessons.controlled: Unscramble p. 47 items. Match each to a body part; model a pair of goggles/boots and a helmet.
lessons.guided: Read p. 51 and match headings; listen twice to U3-A and note four facts about the training scene.
lessons.task: Equipment information desk: identify three pictured items and explain the body part each protects. Partner asks one clarification question.
lessons.check: p. 47 unscrambling; p. 51 headings 1-3; U3-A speaker, setting, goggles/body part, boots/body part.
lessons.answers: gloves, boots, helmet, goggles, overalls, mask (correct the extra letter in the printed boots scramble). Headings: 1-B, 2-C, 3-A. U3-A: Nasser; training workshop; eyes; feet.
lessons.exitq: Complete: Goggles protect the ___. A helmet protects the ___.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: eyes; head.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse equipment names and singular/plural agreement.
lessons.support: Use picture-word-body cards and practise one item versus a pair.
lessons.nextstep: Ask learners to identify two new pictures and make full sentences.
lessons.home: Answer p. 52 short questions; label five equipment pictures. This is language study; practical PPE selection follows college training.
lessons.prior: Basic spoken English and familiar college/workplace experiences; diagnose in the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Explain safety signs and rules
lessons.outcome: Explain a safety message using must or mustn't and distinguish a rule from advice.
lessons.criteria: Interpret four written sign messages; retrieve 3/4 facts from Ali's text; give two rules and one advice sentence
lessons.vocab: mandatory = required; prohibition = something not allowed; warning = message about danger; precaution = action to reduce risk; must = strong requirement; should = advice.
lessons.model: You must follow the safety signs. You mustn't enter a restricted area. You should ask your trainer if a message is unclear. Mustn't means prohibited.
lessons.ccq: Does mustn't mean optional or prohibited? Prohibited. Is should usually advice or a strict requirement? Advice.
lessons.lead: Display the written labels No entry, Wear eye protection, First aid and Warning. Learners predict each message.
lessons.controlled: Match the four companion labels to meanings. Read p. 70 and sort sentences as requirement, prohibition or advice.
lessons.guided: Read pp. 56-57; answer the four companion text questions. Underline the evidence before comparing answers.
lessons.task: Pairs create a spoken orientation for a fictional workshop: two rules and one piece of advice. Explain the meaning rather than demonstrate equipment use.
lessons.check: Labels: No entry / Wear eye protection / First aid / Warning. Ali: workshop? eyes protected by? behaviour near high voltage? two character words?
lessons.answers: Do not enter; required eye protection; place where help/supplies are available; danger to notice. Ali: automotive; goggles; stays away unless trained and authorised; responsible and careful.
lessons.exitq: Complete: You ___ ignore safety signs. You ___ ask for help if instructions are unclear.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: mustn't. 1 point: should. Accept must in item 2 if learner clearly presents it as a stated site rule.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse mustn't with do not have to.
lessons.support: Use required / prohibited / advice headings with a clear example under each.
lessons.nextstep: Present one new rule and one new advice sentence; ask for meaning and form.
lessons.home: Write four sentences from p. 71 signs; use Give way rather than the printed Give away.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Read about marine safety and plurals
lessons.outcome: Identify marine safety vocabulary and use singular and plural nouns accurately.
lessons.criteria: Match 4/4 marine equipment definitions; form 4/5 plurals; report two equipment functions from the text
lessons.vocab: lifejacket = wearable buoyancy aid; lifebuoy = floating ring for rescue; immersion suit = protective suit for cold-water emergencies; lifeline = safety rope; emergency = urgent dangerous situation.
lessons.model: One lifejacket; two lifejackets. One foot; two feet. One injury; two injuries. A lifejacket helps a person float. These are vocabulary examples, not rescue training.
lessons.ccq: Is feet singular or plural? Plural. Is includes a plural noun? No; it is a verb form.
lessons.lead: Show the four equipment pictures on p. 59. Ask which item is worn and which is ring-shaped.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 62 and match p. 59 definitions. Complete the five companion plural forms using pp. 68-69.
lessons.guided: Listen to U3-B: note where the demonstration is, who gives instructions and whom to tell about a problem. Verify with a second listening.
lessons.task: Maritime visitor briefing: explain two equipment names/functions and relay a clear request for help. Keep it a seated language role-play.
lessons.check: p. 59 matching; plural of glove, box, injury, foot, body. p. 62: equipment named? who explains rules? U3-B: three details?
lessons.answers: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c. gloves, boxes, injuries, feet, bodies. Text: lifejackets, first aid kit, radio; captain. U3-B: training room; instructor; instructor.
lessons.exitq: Write the plurals of foot and injury. Add one correct marine equipment word.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point if both plurals are correct: feet, injuries. 1 point for a correctly spelled marine item, e.g. lifejacket.
lessons.barrier: Learners add -s to every noun.
lessons.support: Use regular / -ies / irregular columns and one new example in each.
lessons.nextstep: Check a new regular plural and one irregular form without the word bank.
lessons.home: Complete p. 69 noun choices; answer p. 62 questions 1-5 using the passage.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Make polite requests and respond
lessons.outcome: Make and respond to a polite classroom or workplace request.
lessons.criteria: Match 5/6 request situations; distinguish acceptance from refusal in 3/4 spoken turns; complete a four-turn request exchange
lessons.vocab: request = polite asking; permission = approval to do something; borrow = use and return; lend = give temporarily; refusal = polite no; certainly = yes, willingly.
lessons.model: A: Could I borrow your calculator, please? B: Sorry, I'm using it. A: Could I use it later? B: Certainly. Practise a polite rising tone.
lessons.ccq: If I borrow a pen, do I keep it forever? No. Does Sorry, I'm using it mean acceptance? No.
lessons.lead: Act out a direct Give me a pen and a polite Could I borrow your pen, please? Learners compare the language.
lessons.controlled: Complete p. 66 matching 1-6 and p. 67 requests/refusals. Explain why each response fits.
lessons.guided: Listen to U3-C turns and label accept/refuse. Practise each request with two different responses.
lessons.task: Resource-sharing role-play using pens, a calculator, a book and a chair. Each learner requests twice, accepts once and politely refuses once with a reason.
lessons.check: p. 66 matching 1-6; p. 67 refusals 1-5. U3-C four responses: acceptance or refusal?
lessons.answers: p. 66: 1-D, 2-B, 3-A, 4-C, 5-E, 6-F. p. 67: 1-E, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C, 5-B. U3-C: accept, refuse, accept, refuse.
lessons.exitq: Write a polite request to borrow a pen and a suitable refusal.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: Can/Could I borrow your pen, please? 1 point: Sorry, I'm using it, or a similarly suitable refusal.
lessons.barrier: Learners use yes or no alone and miss polite follow-up language.
lessons.support: Provide a request / response / reason frame, then remove one line during rehearsal.
lessons.nextstep: Ask for a new request and a refusal with a reason using a different object.
lessons.home: Write two request-response pairs for the situations on pp. 64-65; no practical demonstration needed.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Create a clear safety message
lessons.outcome: Produce and explain a short safety notice with equipment vocabulary, rules and advice.
lessons.criteria: Correct four noun/modal errors; plan two rules and two advice points; create a six-sentence notice and explain it
lessons.vocab: notice = short written message; audience = intended readers/listeners; rule = required behaviour; advice = recommendation; clear = easy to understand.
lessons.model: Read the signs before entering. You must follow the trainer's instructions. You mustn't enter restricted areas. You should ask if a rule is unclear.
lessons.ccq: Does a good notice need a clear reader and place? Yes. After must, do we use wear or wears? Wear.
lessons.lead: Retrieve three equipment/body-part pairs and the meanings of must, mustn't and should.
lessons.controlled: Edit the four companion errors. Use the model notice to identify rule, prohibition and advice.
lessons.guided: Plan a notice for a fictional college training room: heading, two equipment sentences, two rules and two advice sentences.
lessons.task: Write six sentences and a heading. Explain the notice to a partner who asks one clarification question. Assess language and clarity with the unit rubric.
lessons.check: Correct: 1 two foots; 2 Goggles protects eyes; 3 You must wears a helmet; 4 You should to ask your trainer.
lessons.answers: two feet; Goggles protect eyes/the eyes; You must wear a helmet; You should ask your trainer. Any equipment requirement must match the stated scenario/site instruction.
lessons.exitq: Write one accurate mustn't rule and one sentence using a plural equipment/body-part word.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each for correct meaning and grammar. Example: You mustn't ignore signs. Goggles protect the eyes. Score full notice separately /10.
lessons.barrier: Learners write vague slogans instead of specific messages.
lessons.support: Give one clear place/audience and sentence frames, then check every sentence says something useful.
lessons.nextstep: Use a new sign to check whether learners can independently express the rule.
lessons.home: Revise the notice after feedback and add one correct polite request.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

inputs: U3-A | Equipment vocabulary | Sunday

My name is Nasser. I am in a training workshop. Today our trainer explains protective equipment. Goggles protect the eyes, and boots protect the feet. The trainer shows us how equipment is chosen for a particular task. We ask questions when a label is unclear.
Questions: Name? Setting? Goggles protect what? Boots protect what?
Key: Nasser; training workshop; eyes; feet.
U3-B | Marine training | Tuesday

Our marine safety lesson is in the training room today. The instructor shows us a lifejacket and a lifebuoy. We listen to the instructor's instructions. If we notice a problem with the training equipment, we tell the instructor. We practise the vocabulary using pictures.
Questions: Where is the lesson? Who gives instructions? Whom do learners tell about a problem?
Key: training room; instructor; instructor. Seated language activity only.
U3-C | Requests | Wednesday

One: Could I borrow your pen? Certainly, here you are. Two: Could I use your calculator? Sorry, I am using it. Three: Can I share your book? Of course. Four: Could I use your phone? I am afraid it is not working.
Task: Label each response acceptance or refusal. Then change one refusal into a polite acceptance.
Key: accept; refuse; accept; refuse.
card: SAFETY LANGUAGE CARD

Required: You must follow the trainer's instructions. Prohibited: You mustn't ignore warning signs. Advice: You should ask if a label is unclear. Advice against: You shouldn't guess the meaning of an unfamiliar sign. Use approved task-specific equipment and college procedures. Do not infer that any ordinary glove, mask or pair of goggles suits every hazard.
resources.model: Goggles protect the eyes. Boots protect the feet. You must follow the trainer's instructions. You mustn't enter restricted areas. You should ask if a sign is unclear. You shouldn't guess the meaning of a warning.
rubric: Six clear sentences linked to the stated audience
Accurate equipment names and body parts
Two clear rules using must/mustn't
Two appropriate advice sentences using should/shouldn't
Accurate plurals and an understandable spoken explanation
resources.quick: 1. One foot, two ___. 2. You must ___ (wear/wears) the approved equipment. 3. Mustn't means optional or prohibited? 4. Write a polite request to borrow a book.
resources.quickkey: 1 feet; 2 wear; 3 prohibited; 4 Can/Could I borrow your book, please?
resources.feedback: Your rules are clear. Check plural nouns and use the base verb after must or should.

units.name: Personal Information
units.focus: Profiles, family and work relationships, appearance, possessives and object pronouns.

lessons.title: Listen for personal information
lessons.outcome: Record relevant personal details and introduce a person using accurate simple-present forms.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 4/5 profile details; complete 4/5 present-simple forms; introduce a person using three accurate facts
lessons.vocab: nationality = national identity; occupation = job; hobby = enjoyable free-time activity; experience = knowledge gained through doing; skill = ability.
lessons.model: Mariam is Omani. She studies electronics. She lives in Salalah and enjoys drawing. He works; she studies; they live.
lessons.ccq: Is Salalah a nationality or a city? A city. Do we say she study or she studies? She studies.
lessons.lead: Sort the p. 74 word cloud into personal information and unrelated words. Invite fictional details instead of private information.
lessons.controlled: Complete p. 79 A1-5. Underline the subject and circle the verb ending.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U4-A and complete name, city, study, hobby and future goal. Compare notes before listening again.
lessons.task: Introduce the fictional speaker to a new classmate using three details; partner checks the notes and asks one question.
lessons.check: p. 79 A1-5; U4-A five profile details.
lessons.answers: works; studies; live; employs; speak. U4-A: Mariam; Salalah; electronics; drawing; become a technician.
lessons.exitq: Complete: She ___ (study) electronics. Write one true detail from the listening.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: studies. 1 point: accurate listening detail. Example: She lives in Salalah.
lessons.barrier: Learners hear a word but place it in the wrong form field.
lessons.support: Preview the five headings and predict the type of answer, such as a place or activity.
lessons.nextstep: Read a new three-sentence profile and check a fresh name/place/study grid.
lessons.home: Read Meet the New Team on pp. 77-78; identify one job and one hobby for each person.
lessons.prior: Basic spoken English and familiar college/workplace experiences; diagnose in the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Complete a form and introduce a partner
lessons.outcome: Transfer profile facts into a form and introduce a partner using a suitable object pronoun.
lessons.criteria: Answer 4/5 selected profile items; transfer four facts to a form; introduce a partner and use one object pronoun
lessons.vocab: form = document with information fields; field = space for one detail; hometown = place of origin; object pronoun = me/you/him/her/it/us/them after a verb or preposition; goal = an aim.
lessons.model: This is Salim. He studies engineering. I study with him. This is his notebook. Contrast he as subject with him after with.
lessons.ccq: In I help her, does her do the helping? No, I do. In her notebook, is her followed by a noun? Yes.
lessons.lead: Show four blank form headings. Learners suggest a suitable question for each.
lessons.controlled: Read pp. 77-78; complete T/F1-3 and MC4-5. Locate the evidence for each answer.
lessons.guided: Use the fictional profile card in the input bank to complete four fields. Practise p. 83 object pronouns with I help him/her/them.
lessons.task: Interview a partner using p. 82 prompts with chosen or fictional information. Give a short introduction and one sentence about working with the partner.
lessons.check: p. 78 items 1-5. Replace objects: I help Ali; We know Sara and Noor; She speaks to me and Ali. Profile card fields: name/city/study/hobby.
lessons.answers: T,F,T; 4 c; 5 a. I help him; We know them; She speaks to us. Card: Salim; Sohar; mechanical engineering; football.
lessons.exitq: Replace Ali: I help Ali. Complete: This is Sara. ___ hobby is reading.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: I help him; Her.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse subject pronouns, object pronouns and possessive adjectives.
lessons.support: Use three columns: she / help her / her book. Keep the noun visible after possessive adjectives.
lessons.nextstep: Ask learners to complete he / help ___ / ___ book with fresh examples.
lessons.home: Write the p. 84 partner paragraph using only information the partner chose to share.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Describe family relationships
lessons.outcome: Explain relationships in a fictional family using possessive forms and clear pronoun reference.
lessons.criteria: Match 4/5 family words; retrieve four relationships from listening; explain three relationships with clear possessives
lessons.vocab: siblings = brothers and sisters; cousin = aunt's/uncle's child; aunt = parent's sister; uncle = parent's brother; grandparents = parents of a parent.
lessons.model: Omar is Sara's brother. Their mother is Amal. Sara's aunt is Huda. She is Amal's sister. Possessive 's shows a relationship here.
lessons.ccq: Is my aunt my mother's sister or my sister's daughter? My mother's sister. Who does their refer to in Their mother is Amal? Sara and Omar.
lessons.lead: Build a small fictional family on the board with named boxes; elicit mother, father, brother and sister.
lessons.controlled: Match p. 85 family vocabulary. Convert two of-phrases into possessive 's phrases.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U4-B and draw the family connections. In pairs, check each relationship using a complete sentence.
lessons.task: Information gap: each partner hides one name in the fictional family and asks questions to complete the other's notes; explain three relationships.
lessons.check: p. 85 matching 1-5. U4-B: Sara's brother, mother, aunt and cousin? Rewrite the brother of Sara.
lessons.answers: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c, 5-e. Omar; Amal; Huda; Yousuf. Sara's brother. Their mother refers to Sara and Omar's mother.
lessons.exitq: Complete: Huda is Amal's sister, so Huda is Sara's ___. Rewrite: the mother of Omar.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: aunt; Omar's mother.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse family vocabulary or attach 's to the wrong person.
lessons.support: Use arrows and colour-coded family branches; offer the fictional family instead of personal disclosure.
lessons.nextstep: Give one new family relationship and ask learners to describe it in two ways.
lessons.home: Write four sentences about a real or fictional family; underline possessive 's and their.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Describe people at work
lessons.outcome: Identify workplace roles and describe appearance and personality with accurate pronouns.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 4/5 workplace facts; complete 4/5 pronoun/possessive choices; give a respectful description with three details
lessons.vocab: trainee = person learning a job; supervisor = person guiding work; manager = person responsible for a team; appearance = how someone looks; personality = usual behaviour and qualities.
lessons.model: Mohammed is the manager. He is tall and friendly. His colleague is Raj. Ahmed works with him. Tall describes appearance; friendly describes personality.
lessons.ccq: Is friendly an appearance word? No, a personality word. In his office, what comes after his? A noun.
lessons.lead: Sort tall, friendly, short hair, patient and glasses into appearance/personality.
lessons.controlled: Read Ahmed's First Day on p. 91. Answer p. 92 A1-2 and B3-5.
lessons.guided: Complete the five companion pronoun choices; compare with pp. 94-95. Avoid the ambiguous synonym/antonym task on p. 93.
lessons.task: Staff-directory role-play: describe a fictional colleague with role, one appearance detail and one quality. Partner identifies the correct description and asks a question.
lessons.check: p. 92 A1-2, B3-5. Choose: 1 ___ office (he/his); 2 help ___ (she/her); 3 ___ work together (we/us); 4 ___ colleagues (they/their); 5 speak to ___ (he/him).
lessons.answers: b; b; work card; manager; Are you ready to learn about cars? Grammar: his, her, we, their, him. Roles: Ahmed-trainee; Sarah-Human Resources; Mohammed-manager; Raj-supervisor.
lessons.exitq: Complete: Ali is friendly. ___ hair is short. I work with ___.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each: His; him.
lessons.barrier: Learners use he where a possessive adjective or object pronoun is needed.
lessons.support: Ask Is a noun coming next? and Is the word after with/help? Use sentence cards.
lessons.nextstep: Check her/her with two differently structured sentences and ask learners to explain the role.
lessons.home: Read Sami's profile on p. 97 and answer the five questions; prepare a profile plan.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Write a clear personal profile
lessons.outcome: Write and present a coherent profile of a real or fictional person.
lessons.criteria: Correct four profile errors; plan at least five relevant facts; write 6-8 connected sentences and answer a question
lessons.vocab: profile = short description of a person; background = basic personal history; characteristic = feature or quality; organise = arrange clearly; proofread = check the final writing.
lessons.model: This is Noor. She is a college student from Salalah. She studies electronics. Her hobby is drawing. She is patient and friendly. I enjoy working with her.
lessons.ccq: Does every sentence need to begin with the person's name? No, use clear pronouns. Can you choose a fictional person? Yes.
lessons.lead: Retrieve three profile categories and one example of a subject/object/possessive form.
lessons.controlled: Edit the four companion sentences. Identify the five categories in the unit model.
lessons.guided: Plan identity, study/work, hometown, appearance or interests, and personality. Partner checks whether each fact is clear and appropriate to share.
lessons.task: Write 6-8 connected sentences based on p. 98 or p. 84. Give a short introduction and answer one question. Use the unit rubric for the complete product.
lessons.check: Correct: 1 She study electronics. 2 Him hobby is reading. 3 I work with she. 4 sara is from oman.
lessons.answers: She studies electronics. His hobby is reading. I work with her. Sara is from Oman.
lessons.exitq: Write one accurate sentence about a person using a possessive adjective and one using an object pronoun.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each. Example: Her hobby is reading. I help her. Score full profile separately /10.
lessons.barrier: Learners produce an unconnected list or change pronouns without a clear reference.
lessons.support: Use an identity-to-details order and draw an arrow from each pronoun to its noun.
lessons.nextstep: Revisit the most common profile error before moving to routine descriptions.
lessons.home: Revise the profile; underline one possessive adjective and circle one object pronoun.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

inputs: U4-A | A fictional student profile | Sunday
Mariam is a student from Salalah. She studies electronics at a vocational college. Her hobby is drawing. She is patient and enjoys group projects. In the future, she wants to become a technician.
Task: Record name, city, study, hobby and future goal.
Key: Mariam; Salalah; electronics; drawing; become a technician.
U4-B | A fictional family | Tuesday
Sara and Omar are siblings. Their mother is Amal and their father is Khalid. Amal has a sister called Huda. Huda is married to Nabil. They have a son called Yousuf. Yousuf is Sara and Omar's cousin.
Questions: Who is Sara's brother? Mother? Aunt? Cousin? Who does their in Their mother refer to?
Key: Omar; Amal; Huda; Yousuf; Sara and Omar.
card: PROFILE CARD | MONDAY

Salim: hometown Sohar; studies mechanical engineering; hobby football; personality patient and helpful. Partner A asks questions; Partner B answers as Salim. Use only these supplied details or label additions as fictional. Real learners can choose what to share and omit contact details.
extra: Subject: She helps. Object: I help her. Possessive adjective + noun: her notebook. Possessive relationship: Sara's brother. Contrast He works / I work with him / His office. With her, the form is the same for object and possessive adjective; the sentence position and following noun show its job.
resources.model: This is Noor. She is a college student from Salalah. She studies electronics. Her hobby is drawing. She has dark hair and wears glasses. She is patient and friendly. I enjoy working with her because she listens carefully. She wants to become a technician.
rubric: At least five relevant, appropriate profile details
Six to eight connected sentences in a clear order
Accurate present-simple verbs and subject pronouns
Clear possessive adjectives and object pronouns
Respectful description, punctuation and spoken response
resources.quick: 1. She ___ (study) English. 2. I work with ___ (he/him). 3. ___ hobby is drawing (she/her). 4. Your aunt's child is your ___.
resources.feedback: The reader understands who you describe. Check whether the next word is a noun before choosing his/her/their.

units.name: Daily Work Routine
units.focus: Work/study routines, present simple, frequency, time expressions and sequence words.

lessons.title: Read and describe a college routine
lessons.outcome: Describe a college routine in a logical sequence with accurate simple-present verbs.
lessons.criteria: Match 4/5 paragraph headings; retrieve 3/4 routine facts; retell four events in order
lessons.vocab: routine = regular pattern of activities; theory = ideas learned about a subject; practical = involving doing; diagnose = identify a problem; repair = fix something.
lessons.model: Hamzah wakes up at six. He takes the bus to college. His classes start at half past eight. He studies car systems and practises in the workshop.
lessons.ccq: Does a daily routine describe one unusual event or repeated events? Repeated events. Is it he wake or he wakes? He wakes.
lessons.lead: Learners list three morning activities and put them in a sensible order.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 101 and match the five headings on p. 102. Explain the key idea of each paragraph.
lessons.guided: Find four routine facts in the companion check; use p. 114 to contrast I wake/he wakes and do/does.
lessons.task: Explain Hamzah's day to a new student using a four-event timeline. Partner asks two questions about time or activity.
lessons.check: p. 102 headings A-E. When does Hamzah wake up, how does he travel, when do classes start, and what does he do after regular classes?
lessons.answers: Headings: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-5, E-4. Wakes 6 a.m.; bus; classes 8:30 a.m.; often practises in the workshop until 5:30 p.m. These are text details, not the college's current timetable.
lessons.exitq: Complete: He ___ (wake) at six. Write one accurate fact from Hamzah's routine.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: wakes. 1 point: accurate text fact.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse time expressions with the activity itself.
lessons.support: Use two timeline rows: time above, action below; model one entry.
lessons.nextstep: Give a new short timetable and ask learners for one complete event sentence.
lessons.home: Complete p. 114 A and B; write three sentences comparing your routine with Hamzah's.
lessons.prior: Basic spoken English and familiar college/workplace experiences; diagnose in the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Ask about work and study schedules
lessons.outcome: Listen for schedule details and ask simple-present questions about routines.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 4/5 listening details; form 4/5 do/does questions; interview a partner and report two facts
lessons.vocab: schedule = plan with times; shift = period of work; colleague = person you work with; project = planned piece of work; marine = related to the sea.
lessons.model: What time does Huda start class? She starts at eight. Does she study in the library? Yes, she does. What do you study? I study English.
lessons.ccq: After does, do we use starts or start? Start. Does does go with she? Yes.
lessons.lead: Retrieve he/she verb endings and ask learners to convert one routine statement into a question.
lessons.controlled: Complete the five do/does/base-verb items in the companion check using p. 114.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U5-A and U5-B. Record selected study/time details, then compare the two routines.
lessons.task: Schedule interview: ask when/where/what and one yes-no question. Record a partner's chosen answers and report two accurate facts.
lessons.check: 1 ___ she start at eight? 2 ___ you take the bus? 3 What does he ___ (study)? 4 She ___ (not/work) on Friday. 5 They ___ (not/start) at seven. U5-A and U5-B details?
lessons.answers: Does; Do; study; doesn't work; don't start. U5-A: Huda, bus, class 8 a.m., lunch 1 p.m., library after class. U5-B: Salim, marine engineering, ship design, computers, engine lesson after lunch.
lessons.exitq: Correct: Does she studies English? Then write a short positive answer.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: Does she study English? 1 point: Yes, she does.
lessons.barrier: Learners keep -s on the main verb after does.
lessons.support: Move the -s idea to does with word cards; leave the main verb in its base form.
lessons.nextstep: Ask learners to form a question with he and a new verb, then answer it.
lessons.home: Read Sarah's work routine on pp. 104-105 and answer the three short questions.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Tell the time and explain frequency
lessons.outcome: Describe a work schedule using clock times, frequency adverbs and in/on/at.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve four schedule facts; choose 4/5 time/frequency forms; describe three routine events with clear times
lessons.vocab: frequency = how often; usually = on most occasions; rarely = not often; quarter = fifteen minutes in time phrases; half past = thirty minutes after an hour.
lessons.model: Nabeel starts work at seven. He usually has toast for breakfast. He does not work on weekends. At 6:45 means at a quarter to seven.
lessons.ccq: Does rarely mean every time? No. Is 6:45 a quarter past six or a quarter to seven? A quarter to seven.
lessons.lead: Write 7:00, 4:30 and 6:45; learners give digital or spoken forms before practising both.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 109 and retrieve breakfast/start/lunch/end times. Say each time aloud.
lessons.guided: Use pp. 115-117 to complete the five companion choices; compare adverb position before main verbs and after be.
lessons.task: Plan a fictional workday in pairs. Explain three time/activity entries and ask a partner how often they do two activities.
lessons.check: Nabeel: breakfast, start, lunch, finish? Complete: 1 ___ 7:00; 2 ___ Sunday; 3 ___ the morning; 4 She ___ checks tools (usually/is usually); 5 She is ___ late (never/does never).
lessons.answers: 6 a.m.; 7 a.m.; noon; 4 p.m. Forms: at; on; in; usually; never. Frequency percentages in the book are illustrations, not exact dictionary meanings.
lessons.exitq: Write 4:30 in words and complete: I study English ___ Sunday.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: half past four/four thirty. 1 point: on.
lessons.barrier: Learners mix past/to and put frequency words in the wrong position.
lessons.support: Use a drawn clock and colour the subject/be/main verb before placing the adverb.
lessons.nextstep: Check one new clock time and one frequency sentence with be.
lessons.home: Complete p. 116 B and write four routine sentences with different frequency adverbs.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Sequence tasks and discuss a workday
lessons.outcome: Put spoken activities in order and discuss a regular work routine using clear sequence words.
lessons.criteria: Order 4/5 spoken activities; choose correct present-simple forms; explain a five-step routine and ask two questions
lessons.vocab: sequence = order of events; first = beginning; next/then = following step; finally = last step; duty = work responsibility; check = examine.
lessons.model: First, I arrive at college. Next, I read the schedule. Then, I attend class. After that, I study in the library. Finally, I go home.
lessons.ccq: Does finally introduce the first or last event? Last. Do we use Do you...? to ask about a regular routine? Yes.
lessons.lead: Mix up five familiar study activities; learners explain a sensible order.
lessons.controlled: Review p. 114 forms with the four companion corrections. Identify sequence words on p. 119.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U5-C and number the five activities. Practise p. 113 role cards as usual training duties, rather than completed past work.
lessons.task: Supervisor/trainee language role-play: explain a regular day and ask two Do you...? questions. Use cards and spoken descriptions only.
lessons.check: Correct: 1 He don't work; 2 Does they start early? 3 She usually is late; 4 He doesn't checks tools. U5-C order?
lessons.answers: He doesn't work. Do they start early? She is usually late. He doesn't check tools. U5-C: arrive, read schedule, attend class, study in library, go home.
lessons.exitq: Write the first and last sentences of a sensible routine using First and Finally.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point per correctly ordered, understandable present-simple sentence with the specified marker.
lessons.barrier: Learners use sequence words but place the events in an illogical order.
lessons.support: Sequence picture/word cards first; add connectors only after the order is agreed.
lessons.nextstep: Give a fresh four-event routine and ask for an independent ordered explanation.
lessons.home: Make a five-event plan for Thursday's routine paragraph, including times and frequency.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Write and present a daily routine
lessons.outcome: Write a coherent routine paragraph and present its main events with clear time expressions.
lessons.criteria: Correct four routine errors; plan five ordered events with times; write 7-9 connected sentences using frequency and sequence
lessons.vocab: topic sentence = sentence introducing the paragraph; time expression = phrase saying when; transition = link between ideas; routine paragraph = connected description of regular activities.
lessons.model: I am a vocational college student. First, I wake up at six. Next, I have breakfast. I usually take the bus at seven. Finally, I go to bed at ten.
lessons.ccq: Are these events repeated or a single past story? Repeated. Does after that link to an earlier event? Yes.
lessons.lead: Retrieve five sequence markers and three time prepositions; use one of each in a sentence.
lessons.controlled: Correct the companion examples; identify the topic sentence and transitions in the unit model.
lessons.guided: Use p. 120 to plan a personal routine or p. 123 for a fictional routine. Include five events, three times and two frequency adverbs.
lessons.task: Write 7-9 connected sentences; include first, next, then, after that and finally where natural. Present the main routine, then peer-edit time and verb forms. Assess with the unit rubric.
lessons.check: Correct: 1 He wake up at six. 2 I have lunch on noon. 3 She doesn't studies at night. 4 Finally, I get up. First, I sleep. (Correct the order.)
lessons.answers: He wakes up at six. I have lunch at noon. She doesn't study at night. First, I get up. Finally, I go to sleep. Accept a coherent equivalent routine.
lessons.exitq: Write one revised routine sentence and explain one correction you made.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: accurate revised sentence. 1 point: valid explanation, e.g. use at before a clock time. Full paragraph scored separately /10.
lessons.barrier: Learners omit time links or shift from present to past within the routine.
lessons.support: Use a time/action planner and highlight all verbs before drafting; keep the subject consistent.
lessons.nextstep: Use the portfolio to choose one course-wide priority, model it and collect a fresh short description.
lessons.home: Submit the revised paragraph with one personal learning target for the next course.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

inputs: U5-A | Huda's college day | Monday
Huda takes the bus to college. Her first class starts at eight in the morning. She studies English before lunch. She has lunch at one o'clock. After her classes, she usually studies in the library.
Task: Record speaker, transport, first-class time, lunch time and after-class place.
Key: Huda; bus; 8 a.m.; 1 p.m.; library.
U5-B | Marine studies | Monday

Salim studies marine engineering. In the morning, he has a ship-design lesson. The students use computers to draw their designs. After lunch, Salim has an engine lesson. He enjoys learning with his classmates.
Task: Record name, specialisation, morning lesson, design tool and afternoon lesson.
Key: Salim; marine engineering; ship design; computers; engine lesson.
U5-C | A five-event study routine | Wednesday
First, I arrive at college. Next, I read the schedule. Then, I attend my class. After that, I study in the library. Finally, I go home.
Task: Number: go home / attend class / arrive / study in library / read schedule.
card: TIME AND FREQUENCY CARD

6:45 = six forty-five / a quarter to seven; 4:30 = four thirty / half past four. Use at with clock times, on with days/dates, in with months/years/parts of the day. Usually/often/sometimes/rarely show approximate frequency, not fixed percentages. Before the main verb: She often studies. After be: She is rarely late.
resources.model: I am a vocational college student. First, I wake up at six in the morning. Next, I have breakfast with my family. Then, I take the bus at seven. My first class starts at eight. I usually study English in the morning. After that, I have lunch and attend another class. I often do my homework in the evening. Finally, I go to bed at ten.
rubric: Clear topic and at least five logically ordered events
Seven to nine connected sentences
Accurate present-simple verbs and consistent subject
Three clear times and two frequency adverbs
Appropriate sequence words, punctuation and spoken summary
resources.quick: 1. Does she ___ (study/studies)? 2. ___ Sunday (in/on/at). 3. Change 6:45 into words. 4. Correct: She usually is early.
resources.quickkey: 1 study; 2 on; 3 six forty-five/a quarter to seven; 4 She is usually early.
resources.feedback: Your routine is easy to follow. Check verb endings and place the frequency adverb before a main verb but after be.

units.name: Machines and Tools
units.focus: Departments, tool functions, marine navigation, drafting, business vocabulary, linking words and locations.

lessons.title: Choose a department; name its tools
lessons.outcome: Identify common tools and explain a department choice with a reason.
lessons.criteria: Name 6/8 selected items; retrieve 3/4 listening details; give a choice plus a reason.
lessons.prior: Common jobs; simple present; I like...
lessons.vocab: department = a study area; spanner = tool for nuts and bolts; drill = tool for holes; helmet = protective headwear.
lessons.model: I want to study Automotive Technologies because I like repairing cars. A spanner is used to tighten nuts.
lessons.ccq: Does a drill make holes or measure length? Holes.
lessons.lead: Use p. 3 pictures. Learners name a familiar department and one job connected to it.
lessons.controlled: Name eight items from pp. 5-6: saw, gloves, helmet, spanner, screwdriver, hammer, drill and measuring tape. Pair-check spellings.
lessons.guided: Read listening U1-A twice. First identify the department; then record two tools, their functions and one protective item.
lessons.task: Department adviser role-play: visitor asks about a department; adviser names two tools and gives a reason to study it. Swap roles.
lessons.check: 1. Which tool makes holes? 2. Which tool measures length? 3. Complete: I choose ___ because ___.
lessons.answers: 1 drill; 2 measuring tape; 3 any appropriate department and clear reason. U1-A: Energy Engineering; drill/holes; pliers/gripping; goggles.
lessons.exitq: Name one tool and state its function. Add one sentence explaining your department choice.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for an accurate tool/function pair; 1 for a relevant choice and reason. Target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse a department, a job and a tool.
lessons.support: Sort words into three labelled columns; provide picture and sentence prompts.
lessons.extension: Compare two departments using but.
lessons.nextstep: Reteach misclassified words with a three-column sort, then request one new independent example.
lessons.home: Revise eight tool names; complete the department prompts on p. 4.

lessons.title: Marine and automotive workplaces
lessons.outcome: Locate tool functions in a marine text and compare them with automotive workshop information.
lessons.criteria: Answer 4/5 selected reading checks; retrieve 3/4 listening details; explain two tool/function pairs.
lessons.prior: Day 1 tool words; It is used to...
lessons.vocab: anchor = equipment that holds a ship in place; bridge = ship control area; net needle = tool for repairing nets; maintain = keep in working condition.
lessons.model: An anchor keeps a ship steady. A net needle is used to repair fishing nets.
lessons.ccq: Is the bridge a place for controlling the ship or storing nets? Controlling the ship.
lessons.lead: Contrast a ship and a car workshop using textbook pictures. Predict three tools.
lessons.controlled: Read pp. 9-10. Answer p. 10 B1-2 and C3-5 independently; underline evidence before comparing.
lessons.guided: Use U1-B as the listening alternative for pp. 11-12. Listen for purpose, tools, protection and the final check.
lessons.task: Expert pairs: one explains a marine workplace; the other explains an automotive workshop. Agree on one similarity and one difference.
lessons.check: p. 10 B1-2; C3-5. Then ask: What does a net needle do?
lessons.answers: B: 1-b, 2-c. C: 3-F, 4-T, 5-F. Net needle: repair/create fishing nets. U1-B: repair/maintain vehicles; lift/spanner/drill; gloves/goggles; test vehicle.
lessons.exitq: Complete two tool/function pairs: anchor / ___; net needle / ___.
lessons.exitkey: Keeps a ship steady; repairs or creates fishing nets. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Learners copy whole paragraphs instead of finding evidence.
lessons.support: Highlight question keywords and model one short answer.
lessons.extension: Explain why navigation is important using because.
lessons.nextstep: Model locating a keyword in one sentence, then ask a new short question without highlighting.
lessons.home: Use p. 10 E to practise short answers; complete p. 12 reflection in two sentences.

lessons.title: Drafting tools and polite requests
lessons.outcome: Explain drafting-tool functions and make an appropriate request for a tool.
lessons.criteria: Match 4/5 tools to functions; answer 3/4 reading checks; complete a four-turn request with the correct function.
lessons.prior: Tool names and uses; Can you...?
lessons.vocab: drafting = preparing technical drawings; compass = circle-drawing tool; set square = tool for angles; drawing board = surface for drawing.
lessons.model: A: Can you give me the T-square, please? B: What do you want it for? A: I want to draw straight lines. B: Here you are.
lessons.ccq: Does a compass draw circles or straight lines? Circles.
lessons.lead: Show p. 13 tools. Students predict which tool helps draw a circle.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 14. Answer p. 15 A1-4 and match T-square, compass, drawing board, set square and AutoCAD to functions.
lessons.guided: Read U1-C tool clues. Learners identify four tools, then practise the p. 18 dialogue using matching tool/function cards.
lessons.task: Tool-counter information gap: each learner requests two tools for a drawing task; the partner checks the purpose before handing over the word card.
lessons.check: p. 15 A1-4; B5-6. Correct this mismatched request: hacksaw / tighten nuts.
lessons.answers: A: F, T, F, T. B: 5-c (A3/A2), 6-b (AutoCAD). Use a spanner to tighten nuts. U1-C: T-square, compass, drill, spanner.
lessons.exitq: Write a two-line request and purpose for a compass.
lessons.exitkey: Can you give me the compass, please? I want to draw a circle. 1 request point + 1 accurate purpose point.
lessons.barrier: Students pair a correct request with the wrong tool function.
lessons.support: Use colour-matched tool/function cards, then remove the colours.
lessons.extension: Write 40-50 words on whether you would like to be a draftsman, as on p. 16.
lessons.nextstep: Start with two mismatched requests; learners repair them, then create a fresh dialogue.
lessons.home: Complete the p. 16 writing task or improve the version begun in class.

lessons.title: Business ideas and linking words
lessons.outcome: Extract business ideas and connect short statements using addition, contrast, reason and purpose.
lessons.criteria: Explain 3/4 business terms; select 5/7 linking words correctly; present a shop idea with two suitable links.
lessons.prior: Simple sentences; because from Day 1.
lessons.vocab: branding = creating a recognisable product identity; competitors = businesses selling similar products; merchandising = attractive product display; promotion = communicating to help sell.
lessons.model: Our shop sells notebooks and pens. We choose bright colours because customers notice them. We use posters to promote the shop.
lessons.ccq: Does because add another item or give a reason? A reason.
lessons.lead: Ask pairs to invent a name for a stationery shop and say why people might choose it.
lessons.controlled: Skim p. 20 and match the four p. 19 business terms. Complete p. 24 linking-word items 1-7.
lessons.guided: Use p. 22 shop-plan headings: brand, product, place and promotion. Pair-check two sentences for meaning and links.
lessons.task: Give a one-minute shop pitch. Partners choose the clearer pitch and identify one persuasive reason; every learner speaks.
lessons.check: p. 19 A1-4; p. 24 items 1-7. Explain the difference between and and but.
lessons.answers: p. 19: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c. p. 24: and; but; also; In my opinion; to; because; or. And adds information; but contrasts.
lessons.exitq: Join: We sell notebooks. We sell pens. Then complete: We use posters ___ attract customers.
lessons.exitkey: We sell notebooks and pens. to. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students choose links by position rather than meaning.
lessons.support: Label links ADD / CONTRAST / REASON / PURPOSE and use short examples.
lessons.extension: Add people, process and physical evidence to the four-part shop plan; the book lists seven Ps.
lessons.nextstep: Contrast two possible linking words and ask learners to explain how meaning changes.
lessons.home: Complete selected p. 25 linking-word practice; bring five tool/location notes for Thursday.

lessons.title: Give a workshop tour
lessons.outcome: Describe an organised workshop using accurate locations, tool names and linking words.
lessons.criteria: Use four accurate location phrases; describe five items orally; write a coherent 100-150-word paragraph.
lessons.prior: Tool vocabulary, linking words; there is / there are as a familiar support frame.
lessons.vocab: above = higher than; under = lower than; between = in the middle of two things; next to = beside.
lessons.model: There is a toolbox on the workbench. A basket is under it, and the gloves are next to the drill.
lessons.ccq: If the basket is under the bench, is it on top? No.
lessons.lead: Place a pencil beside, under and on a book. Learners describe each position.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 26. Answer p. 27 questions 2-5 and correct the two location/number sentences on the companion page.
lessons.guided: Use the p. 29 or p. 30 image: plan an opening, five item locations and a closing. Check there is / there are and four prepositions.
lessons.task: Give a short tour to a partner, then independently write 100-150 words. Use U1-B resource-page rubric; exchange feedback on one location and one link.
lessons.check: p. 27 Q2-5. Edit: There are a toolbox. The gloves is next to the drill.
lessons.answers: Orange helmet: on the chair. Basket: under the workbench. Wrenches/screwdrivers: on the pegboard. Ear protector: between wrench and yellow helmet. There is a toolbox. The gloves are next to the drill.
lessons.exitq: Write two accurate location sentences about different items in the chosen picture.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for each accurate item + location sentence. Use the writing rubric separately for the full paragraph.
lessons.barrier: Learners list items without organising the description.
lessons.support: Provide opening/location/closing boxes and a short preposition bank.
