lessons.extension: Include a reason for the arrangement and answer a visitor question.
lessons.nextstep: Use the weakest rubric criterion to choose a three-minute revision task before Unit 2.
lessons.home: Revise the paragraph using feedback; complete the alternative picture as optional practice.

inputs: U1-A | Energy Engineering | Sunday

I study Energy Engineering. Today we are learning the names of tools. A drill makes holes. Pliers hold and grip small objects. A measuring tape checks length. We use pictures before our practical lesson. Our instructor shows us goggles and explains their purpose. I enjoy the course because I like finding out how equipment works.
Questions: Which department? Which tool makes holes? Which tool grips? Which protective item is named?
Key: Energy Engineering; drill; pliers; goggles.
U1-B | An automotive workshop | Monday

An automotive workshop repairs and maintains vehicles. Mechanics use a vehicle lift to raise a car, a spanner for nuts and bolts, and a drill to make holes. They discuss the job before they begin. Gloves and goggles are mentioned during the safety briefing. After the repair, the mechanic tests the vehicle before returning it to the owner.
Questions: What is the workshop’s purpose? Name two tools. Name two protective items. What happens after the repair?
Key: repair and maintain vehicles; any two named tools; gloves and goggles; the vehicle is tested.
U1-C | Tool-counter clues | Tuesday

One: I need a tool to draw straight lines on my plan. Two: I need a tool to draw a circle. Three: I need a tool to make a hole. Four: I need a tool to tighten a nut. Choose from a compass, a spanner, a T-square and a drill.
Task: Write the tool for each number. Then make a polite request for two of the tools.
Key: 1 T-square; 2 compass; 3 drill; 4 spanner.
card: A ready-made business prompt

Stationery shop: brand = Bright Pages; products = notebooks and pens; place = near a college; promotion = posters. Ask learners to improve one choice and explain why. This is a fictional classroom business.
resources.model: This is our training workshop. It is bright and organised, and every tool has a place. There is a large workbench in the middle of the room. A toolbox is on the workbench, next to a small drill. The spanners are inside the toolbox, and two screwdrivers are above it on the pegboard. A pair of gloves is beside the drill. Under the workbench, there is a basket for spare materials. A safety helmet is on the chair near the door. We keep the walkway clear because people need space to move. Four accurate location phrases
There is / there are agreement
Suitable linking words and organisation
100-150 words; readable sentences and punctuation
resources.quick: 1. A tool for holes: ___. 2. Choose: a spanner and/because a screwdriver. 3. Correct: There are a helmet. 4. Give one sentence with under.
resources.quickkey: 1 drill; 2 and; 3 There is a helmet; 4 any accurate under sentence.
resources.feedback: Your tool names are clear. Check the two sentences with more than one item: use there are. Then add one reason using because.

units.name: Actions in Workshops
units.focus: Workshop actions, present continuous, there is / there are, spoken and written scene descriptions.

lessons.title: What happens in an automotive workshop?
lessons.outcome: Identify workshop actions and locate supporting details in an automotive text.
lessons.criteria: Match 6/8 action words; answer 4/6 comprehension questions; explain two action/tool links.
lessons.prior: Unit 1 tool names and functions.
lessons.vocab: repair = make something work again; maintain = keep working well; inspect/check = examine; install = put equipment in place ready for use.
lessons.model: Technicians check the cars first. A worker uses a jack to lift the car.
lessons.ccq: Do technicians check for problems before or after the repair? Before.
lessons.lead: Use p. 34 title to predict what workers do. Compare with the first paragraph on p. 35.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 35 and answer its six comprehension questions independently. Underline where each answer is found.
lessons.guided: Build a table: worker / action / tool or object. Complete technician/check/cars; worker/change/wheel; electrician/repair/lights.
lessons.task: Workshop guide pairs explain three jobs to a new student. Listener notes two actions and asks one clarification question.
lessons.check: p. 35 Q1-6: first action, engine part, wheel tools, electrician jobs, protection, clean floor.
lessons.answers: Check cars; spark plugs; jack and wrench; repair lights/install radio; gloves/goggles for protection; keep the floor clean. Accept accurate short paraphrases.
lessons.exitq: State the first workshop action and name one tool used to change a wheel.
lessons.exitkey: Check the car for problems; jack or wrench. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students confuse the action with the name of a worker.
lessons.support: Use three columns: person / verb / object and model one row.
lessons.extension: Explain why workers cooperate using because.
lessons.nextstep: Reteach two confused action/tool pairs using picture matching and one independent sentence.
lessons.home: Learn six action verbs from p. 33; prepare one example from your preferred department.

lessons.title: Actions across vocational departments
lessons.outcome: Classify workshop activities by field and explain how practical training prepares learners for jobs.
lessons.criteria: Match 4/4 activities to fields; answer 2/3 multiple-choice items; give two accurate action/tool pairs.
lessons.prior: Day 1 actions; department names from Unit 1.
lessons.vocab: harvest = collect a crop; tighten = make firmly fixed; drill = make holes; design = plan how something will look or work.
lessons.model: Agriculture students harvest cucumbers. Engineering students tighten nuts with a spanner.
lessons.ccq: Does harvesting mean planting seeds or collecting crops? Collecting crops.
lessons.lead: Match a cucumber, anchor, house plan and spanner to four department labels.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 37 and answer p. 38 A1-3 and B1-4. Find the phrase that supports each match.
lessons.guided: Use p. 36 pictures to complete four rows: field / action / object. Partners explain rather than simply exchange letters.
lessons.task: Department puzzle: describe an activity without naming the field. Partner identifies the field and asks which tool is used. Swap after two clues.
lessons.check: p. 38 A1-3 and B1-4; name the two vegetables in the text.
lessons.answers: A: 1-B, 2-C, 3-B. B: 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D. Vegetables: cucumbers and tomatoes.
lessons.exitq: Match harvesting to its field. Write one accurate engineering action and tool.
lessons.exitkey: Agriculture; e.g., tighten nuts with a spanner or drill metal with a drill. 1 point each.
lessons.barrier: Students rely on pictures without checking the reading.
lessons.support: Require an underlined word or phrase beside every answer.
lessons.extension: Explain one activity shared by more than one department.
lessons.nextstep: Present one disputed match; ask for evidence, then give a new independent matching item.
lessons.home: Complete the two open questions on p. 38 and revise the field/action table.

lessons.title: Describe actions happening now
lessons.outcome: Form affirmative, negative and question sentences about actions happening now.
lessons.criteria: Complete 4/5 verb forms; produce all three sentence types; ask and answer two action questions.
lessons.prior: Action verbs; subjects and am/is/are.
lessons.vocab: now = at this time; affirmative = positive statement; negative = states something is not happening; question = asks for information.
lessons.model: The worker is repairing a car. He is not painting it. Is he using a spanner?
lessons.ccq: Is the repair happening now or every day in this example? Now.
lessons.lead: Mime a familiar non-hazardous action such as writing or measuring; learners describe it.
lessons.controlled: Use p. 43 prompts for worker/repair/car and students/plant/seeds. Make an affirmative, negative and question for each.
lessons.guided: Complete p. 44 C together after an individual attempt. Notice be + verb-ing and subject agreement.
lessons.task: Guess the action: one learner uses a picture card; a partner asks yes/no questions to identify it. Swap; keep two question/answer records.
lessons.check: Complete: Ahmed ___ (write); Fatima and Mariam ___ (talk); the teacher ___ (help); students ___ (play); others ___ (sit).
lessons.answers: is writing; are talking; is helping; are playing; are sitting. p. 44 B: C, A, B. I uses am; he/she/it uses is; you/we/they use are.
lessons.exitq: Correct: He repairing a car. Then turn They are planting seeds into a question.
lessons.exitkey: He is repairing a car. Are they planting seeds? 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students omit be or keep a base verb after it.
lessons.support: Build sentences with subject / be / action-ing cards; remove the cards for exit work.
lessons.extension: Add a negative and explain a contrast with but.
lessons.nextstep: Use one missing-be sentence and one wrong-agreement sentence, then test a new subject.
lessons.home: Complete the remaining p. 44 paragraph forms and write three true actions happening around you.

lessons.title: Who is working where?
lessons.focus: Listening, there is / there are and speaking
lessons.outcome: Identify actions in spoken scenes and describe people using there is / there are with action phrases.
lessons.criteria: Record 6/8 listening action details; complete 4/5 existence forms; give three accurate scene sentences.
lessons.prior: Present continuous; singular/plural nouns; prepositions.
lessons.vocab: scene = what is happening in a place; singular = one; plural = more than one; wiring = connecting electrical components.
lessons.model: There is a student drawing a plan. There are two students planting seeds next to the greenhouse.
lessons.ccq: Do we use is or are with two students? Are.
lessons.lead: Use the p. 45 or p. 46 picture to count people and identify two actions.
lessons.controlled: Read U2-A numbered descriptions twice. Learners record the person, action and object; compare after the second reading.
lessons.guided: Complete p. 42 A1-5 and correct B1-2. Pair descriptions combine a quantity, location and activity.
lessons.task: Information gap: one partner describes a selected part of the textbook scene; the other identifies the people and sketches their position. Swap roles.
lessons.check: p. 42 A1-5. Correct: There is two workers. There are a mechanic.
lessons.answers: There is; There are not/aren’t; Is there; There are; Is there. Corrections: There are two workers. There is a mechanic. U2-A key is on the unit resource page.
lessons.exitq: Describe one person and two people using there is / there are plus an action.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for each accurate number + be + action description; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students mix singular subjects and plural be forms.
lessons.support: Circle the noun/number before choosing is or are; rehearse with two contrasting examples.
lessons.extension: Ask and answer Is there...? and Are there...? questions about the scene.
lessons.nextstep: Start with one-person/two-person contrasts and require new independent examples.
lessons.home: Use p. 45 to write five scene sentences; bring them for Thursday planning.

lessons.title: Write a complete workshop scene
lessons.outcome: Write a connected five- or six-sentence description of a workshop scene and explain it orally.
lessons.criteria: Include an opening and closing; describe at least three actions; use correct number agreement in 4/5 checked sentences.
lessons.prior: Workshop verbs, present continuous, there is / there are, locations.
lessons.vocab: opening = introduces the setting; detail = specific information; closing = finishes the description; revise = improve after checking.
lessons.model: The workshop is busy today. There are two students measuring a board. A teacher is helping them.
lessons.ccq: Does an opening introduce the whole scene or list every detail? The whole scene.
lessons.lead: Review two sentences from Wednesday and improve one together.
lessons.controlled: Edit the three sentences on the companion page; check be and -ing endings.
lessons.guided: Use p. 47: organise an opening, three or four action details and a closing. Check against the U2 writing rubric.
lessons.task: Explain the plan to a partner, then write independently. Exchange a specific comment on action accuracy and revise one sentence.
lessons.check: Edit: There is two students. He is measure wood. They not painting the wall.
lessons.answers: There are two students. He is measuring wood. They are not painting the wall. Accept contractions.
lessons.exitq: Write one new negative action sentence and one there are sentence about the scene.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for each accurate sentence; full description is assessed separately with the U2 rubric.
lessons.barrier: Students produce isolated sentences with no setting or ending.
lessons.support: Use a five-box plan and connect details with and/but/also.
lessons.extension: Add a question and answer about the scene without copying the paragraph.
lessons.nextstep: Use the rubric’s weakest criterion for a short revision task before beginning hazards.
lessons.home: Submit a revised five- or six-sentence paragraph; optional extra picture on p. 45.

inputs: U2-A | Eight workshop scenes | Wednesday

One: A mechanic is fixing an engine. Two: A student is measuring a wooden board. Three: Two students are planting seeds in a tray. Four: A designer is drawing a plan on a computer. Five: A worker is painting a door. Six: Two students are tightening nuts with spanners. Seven: A learner is harvesting cucumbers in a greenhouse. Eight: A technician is connecting electrical components in a training diagram.
Task: Record the person, action and object for each numbered scene. Listen once for the actions, then again for objects. Do not use this key for the original p. 41 recording.
Key actions: 1 fixing; 2 measuring; 3 planting; 4 drawing/designing; 5 painting; 6 tightening; 7 harvesting; 8 connecting/wiring.
card: Ready-to-copy scene card

At the centre: two students measure a board. Beside the window: a teacher helps a learner. On a computer: one student draws a plan. Near the door: two workers organise tools. Use these details for a paper information gap when the textbook image is unavailable.
extra: Present continuous: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. Negative: add not after be. Question: move be before the subject. There is introduces one person/thing; there are introduces more than one. Compare: There are two workers. They are measuring a board.
resources.model: The training workshop is busy this morning. There are two students measuring a wooden board at the large workbench. Beside the window, the teacher is helping a learner, and they are checking a drawing together. A student is using a computer to design a plan, but he is not printing it yet. Near the door, two workers are organising the tools and placing the spanners in a toolbox. Everyone is concentrating on a different task, and the workshop looks organised.
rubric: Clear setting and a suitable closing
At least three relevant action details
Accurate be + verb-ing forms
Accurate there is / there are and locations
Five or six connected, readable sentences
resources.quick: 1. She ___ painting. 2. They ___ not drilling. 3. Correct: There is two workers. 4. Make a question: He is repairing the car.
resources.quickkey: 1 is; 2 are; 3 There are two workers; 4 Is he repairing the car?
resources.feedback: The scene is easy to imagine. Underline each subject and check its be verb. Correct one missing -ing ending, then read the paragraph aloud.

units.name: Hazards in Workshops
units.focus: Accidents, causes, prevention, listening for incident details and inferring vocabulary from context.

lessons.title: Recognise hazards and describe accidents
lessons.outcome: Name common accidents, separate observation from possible cause, and report a concern clearly.
lessons.criteria: Identify 4/5 accident terms; give two plausible causes using may; state a location and problem clearly.
lessons.prior: Present continuous; workshop tools and locations.
lessons.vocab: hazard = possible source of harm; injury = harm to the body; bleeding = losing blood; faint = briefly lose consciousness.
lessons.model: A worker is bleeding in the workshop. A sharp tool may have caused the injury. Please call the first aider.
lessons.ccq: Is a possible cause something we know for certain? No.
lessons.lead: Use p. 50 pictures. Learners say only what they can see before suggesting a possible cause.
lessons.controlled: Match cut, burn, bleeding, fainting and electric shock to p. 50 images or teacher word cards. Distinguish injury from cause.
lessons.guided: Use p. 51 C to write two cautious possibilities. Pair-check observation versus inference.
lessons.task: Reporter and supervisor role-play: give location, visible problem and request for help. Use fictional picture situations; swap roles.
lessons.check: Sort: wet floor / cut hand / damaged wire / bleeding. Which are hazards and which are injury signs?
lessons.answers: Hazards: wet floor, damaged wire. Injury/signs: cut hand, bleeding. Do not claim a guessed cause as fact.
lessons.exitq: Name one hazard and give one clear sentence reporting an accident at a location.
lessons.exitkey: 1 appropriate hazard + 1 clear location/problem sentence = 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students treat guesses about a cause as confirmed facts.
lessons.support: Use I can see... and It may be because... frames.
lessons.extension: Add one prevention message linked to the hazard.
lessons.nextstep: Contrast an observation and a guess; ask learners to label a fresh pair.
lessons.home: Make a five-word hazard glossary with simple definitions. Use language examples, not practical demonstrations.

lessons.title: Listen and report essential incident details
lessons.outcome: Listen for the place, problem and response in an incident report and relay the message accurately.
lessons.criteria: Identify the main problem; retrieve 3/4 details; communicate the place, problem and help needed.
lessons.prior: Hazard vocabulary and reporting frames.
lessons.vocab: first aider = person trained to give first aid; alert = tell someone about danger; response = action taken; witness = person who saw an event.
lessons.model: There is an injured worker near the workbench. He has cut his hand. Please send the first aider.
lessons.ccq: Should a report include an exact place? Yes, so help can find the person.
lessons.lead: Compare a vague message, Something happened, with a clear location/problem message.
lessons.controlled: Listen to U3-A once for the main problem and again for four details. Use its own questions, not the original audio questions.
lessons.guided: Complete a place / person / problem / response note grid; compare notes and repair one missing detail.
lessons.task: Telephone role-play: reporter gives three essential facts; receiver repeats them back and asks one checking question.
lessons.check: U3-A: Where is the worker? What happened? Who was alerted? What happened to the lesson?
lessons.answers: Near the workbench; cut hand/bleeding; trained first aider; the activity stopped and classmates moved away.
lessons.exitq: Write a message including a specific place and a problem/help request.
lessons.exitkey: 1 location point + 1 clear problem/help point. Target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Learners remember the story but omit the location.
lessons.support: Provide three note boxes and practise a short read-back.
lessons.extension: Report the same event in two concise sentences without the grid.
lessons.nextstep: Give a new 20-second incident message; check whether location is recorded independently.
lessons.home: Review five incident words. For the book’s burn item, use the corrected teacher note on the source page.

lessons.title: Read about electrical hazards
lessons.outcome: Find causes and prevention ideas in a safety text and infer meanings from context.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 3/4 cause/prevention details; identify 3/4 word relationships; justify an answer with a text clue.
lessons.prior: Hazard, cause and response; short-answer reading.
lessons.vocab: damaged = broken or harmed; prevent = stop something happening; exposed = not covered; current = flow of electricity.
lessons.model: Damaged wires can cause electric shock. Here, damaged is similar in meaning to broken.
lessons.ccq: Are prevent and cause the same? No; prevent stops something happening.
lessons.lead: Predict why a damaged wire and wet conditions could be mentioned in a safety text.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 53 for causes and prevention; use the updated safety note. Answer the four teacher checks listed on the companion page.
lessons.guided: Use p. 55 synonyms/antonyms: damaged, prevent, safe and dry. Underline the context that supports each answer.
lessons.task: Pairs create a four-item language safety notice: identify two hazards and give two prevention messages from the text. Explain one word choice.
lessons.check: 1 Name two causes. 2 Name one prevention measure. 3 damaged = ? 4 Opposite of dry?
lessons.answers: Damaged wires/faulty equipment/wet conditions; inspect equipment or keep areas dry; broken; wet. p. 55 additional pairs: prevent/avoid, safe/unsafe.
lessons.exitq: Give a synonym for damaged and an antonym for safe.
lessons.exitkey: broken; unsafe. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Learners select a familiar word without using its context.
lessons.support: Read the surrounding sentence; substitute the candidate word and check meaning.
lessons.extension: Use exposed and prevent in two original sentences.
lessons.nextstep: Model substitution with one unfamiliar word; then let learners infer a new item alone.
lessons.home: Write four vocabulary pairs. Treat these lessons as language work; follow college procedures for real incidents.

lessons.title: Explain causes and prevention
lessons.outcome: Explain a plausible hazard/cause relationship and propose a relevant prevention message.
lessons.criteria: Match 3/4 hazards to prevention ideas; distinguish facts from guesses; justify two recommendations.
lessons.prior: Unit 1 because; Unit 2 descriptions; Unit 3 vocabulary.
lessons.vocab: cause = reason something happens; prevention = action that reduces a risk; precaution = action taken in advance; evidence = information supporting an idea.
lessons.model: The walkway is blocked, so people may trip. Keep the walkway clear.
lessons.ccq: Does a prevention message address the same hazard or an unrelated one? The same hazard.
lessons.lead: Show a simple board sketch of a blocked walkway and scattered materials; ask what could happen.
lessons.controlled: Match U3 resource scenarios to relevant messages. Label each sentence as observation, possible cause or prevention.
lessons.guided: Groups complete hazard / possible result / prevention columns for three paper scenarios. Teacher checks logic and wording.
lessons.task: Hold a tabletop safety briefing. Each learner explains one scenario; listeners ask Why? and choose the clearest prevention message.
lessons.check: Match: blocked walkway / damaged tool / unclear instructions / loose materials. Use: ask supervisor; clear route; report tool; organise storage.
lessons.answers: Blocked walkway/clear route; damaged tool/report tool; unclear instructions/ask supervisor; loose materials/organise storage.
lessons.exitq: Write one hazard and one directly related prevention message.
lessons.exitkey: 1 clear hazard + 1 relevant prevention response. Target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students suggest a general rule that does not solve the named problem.
lessons.support: Use matching arrows from each hazard to its specific response.
lessons.extension: Explain two possible consequences without claiming either definitely happened.
lessons.nextstep: Present an irrelevant recommendation; learners replace it and explain why.
lessons.home: Prepare a one-minute briefing using three notes. Written notes are language support, not a new grammar syllabus.

lessons.title: Deliver a clear safety briefing
lessons.outcome: Interpret a short incident and give a clear, evidence-based report and prevention message.
lessons.criteria: Understand 3/4 incident details; use three unit words accurately; report location/problem/help and a relevant prevention idea.
lessons.prior: The week’s cause, report and prevention language.
lessons.vocab: briefing = short explanation of important information; confirm = check accuracy; follow-up = next action; review = check learning again.
lessons.model: The accident happened beside the workbench. A worker cut his hand. The first aider was called. Tools should be stored carefully.
lessons.ccq: Should we add a detail that the witness did not give? No.
lessons.lead: Retrieve three hazard words and one careful reporting phrase from the week.
lessons.controlled: Complete the U3 resource quick check; correct unsupported claims in a sample report.
lessons.guided: Plan a briefing using place / observed problem / help / prevention. Partner checks facts against U3-A, read again if needed.
lessons.task: Deliver a one-minute briefing to a partner and answer a checking question. Independently write a four-line report; apply the U3 rubric.
lessons.check: Identify one observed fact, one possible cause and one prevention message in your report.
lessons.answers: Observed facts must match the source. A cause may be inferred only with may/might. Prevention must address the named hazard.
lessons.exitq: Write a two-sentence report giving the place/problem and a relevant request for help.
lessons.exitkey: 1 accurate place/problem point + 1 relevant help request. Use the unit performance rubric separately.
lessons.barrier: Fluent reports include invented details.
lessons.support: Limit notes to evidence boxes and mark guesses as possible.
lessons.extension: Compare two reports and explain which is more precise.
lessons.nextstep: Choose vocabulary, detail accuracy or clarity for the first review task next week.
lessons.home: Revise the report and retain a vocabulary sample for your learning folder.

inputs: U3-A | A workshop incident | Monday and Thursday

During a classroom workshop activity, a student called for help near the workbench. He had cut his hand, and it was bleeding. The teacher stopped the activity and alerted the trained first aider. The other students moved away so the first aider could reach him. One classmate clearly explained where the student was and what had happened. Later, the class discussed how to report an incident without guessing its cause.
Questions: Where was the student? What was the problem? Who was alerted? What happened to the activity?
Key: near the workbench; cut hand/bleeding; trained first aider; it stopped.
card: Paper scenarios for Wednesday

A: Boxes block a walkway. B: A tool has visible damage. C: A learner does not understand the instructions. D: Loose materials are spread around a storage area. Match with clear the route; report the tool; ask the supervisor; organise storage. Keep these as discussion cards.
extra: The 2024 book includes a 10-minute burn-cooling item. For current language examples, use 20 minutes of cool running water (NHS). For electrical incidents, emphasise keeping clear until the supply is off; isolation must be safe. Use college emergency procedures and trained personnel for practical care. See the clickable references on the final page.
resources.model: The incident happened near the workbench during an activity. A student cut his hand, and it was bleeding. The teacher stopped the activity and called the trained first aider. The classmates moved away and gave a clear description of the location and problem. The exact cause was not confirmed.
rubric: Accurate location, person and problem
Appropriate request or report of help
Clear distinction between fact and possible cause
Accurate use of at least three unit words
Clear delivery and a relevant prevention message
resources.quick: 1. damaged = broken / repaired. 2. Opposite of safe: ___. 3. Is “a wet floor may cause a fall” a confirmed event or possibility? 4. Give one clear help message.
resources.quickkey: 1 broken; 2 unsafe; 3 possibility; 4 accept a specific location, problem and request for the appropriate help.
resources.feedback: You reported the problem clearly. Add the exact location. Change the guessed cause to may have..., or leave it out if you have no evidence.

units.name: Past Events and Stories
units.focus: Narratives, biographies, past simple, past continuous, sequencing and a 100-150-word narrative.

lessons.title: Tell a repair story in the past
lessons.outcome: Understand a short repair narrative and describe completed events using past simple.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 3/4 listening facts; form 4/5 past verbs; give three events in a sensible order.
lessons.prior: Car/workshop vocabulary; present verb forms.
lessons.vocab: alternator = component supplying electrical power; warranty = repair guarantee with conditions; labour = work/service cost; faulty = not working correctly.
lessons.model: Yesterday, the car stopped. Ahmed called a mechanic. He did not drive home. Did the mechanic repair it?
lessons.ccq: After did, do we use went or go? Go.
lessons.lead: Ask learners to predict what might happen when a car stops during a journey.
lessons.controlled: Listen to U4-A for problem and sequence, then four details. Complete p. 76 verb-choice items 1-3.
lessons.guided: Use p. 75 forms and p. 76 paragraph. Change two affirmative sentences to negatives and questions.
lessons.task: Customer/mechanic retelling: explain what happened, what was checked and how it ended. Partner asks a Did...? question.
lessons.check: p. 76 choices and paragraph verbs; U4-A four detail questions.
lessons.answers: Choices: visited, went, wrote. Paragraph: went, decided, brought, ran, ate, talked, enjoyed. U4-A: car stopped; sister; alternator; relieved.
lessons.exitq: Correct: He didn’t went home. Then write one completed repair action.
lessons.exitkey: He didn’t go home. Accept an accurate past-simple repair sentence. 1 point each.
lessons.barrier: Students put past forms after did/didn’t.
lessons.support: Colour-code did + base verb; contrast He went / Did he go?
lessons.extension: Add a reason and a feeling to the repair story.
lessons.nextstep: Start with a three-item did + base correction task, then ask a new question.
lessons.home: Finish p. 76 practice; list five past verbs you can use in a story.

lessons.title: Read a life story
lessons.outcome: Identify main ideas and key events in the Andrew Carnegie biography and retell a short timeline.
lessons.criteria: Match 3/4 headings; answer 3/4 detail questions; retell three accurate events in order.
lessons.prior: Past simple; first/then/later; familiar jobs.
lessons.vocab: factory = place where goods are made; messenger = person delivering messages; invest = put money into an activity for a return; charity = organisation helping people.
lessons.model: Carnegie worked in a cotton factory. Later, he became a messenger. He donated money to libraries and schools.
lessons.ccq: Does later show an earlier event or a following event? A following event.
lessons.lead: Look at the p. 61 pictures and predict a possible life sequence.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 62. Match p. 63 headings A-D, then answer its three multiple-choice questions.
lessons.guided: Use p. 64 E1-2 and create a four-event timeline. Identify four past verbs and classify regular/irregular.
lessons.task: Interview pairs: one is a biographer, one asks about jobs, business and helping others. Use evidence from the text.
lessons.check: p. 63 headings and D1-3; p. 64 E1-2.
lessons.answers: Headings A-5, B-1, C-3, D-2; 4 extra. D: b, b, b. E: learned business/how companies worked; funded libraries, schools and charities.
lessons.exitq: State his first job and one way he helped others.
lessons.exitkey: Cotton factory worker; donated to libraries/schools/charities. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students retell details in the wrong order.
lessons.support: Use four event cards and time connectors; keep dates optional.
lessons.extension: Give an opinion about a decision and support it with one fact from the text.
lessons.nextstep: Reorder three events, then remove cards and ask for a fresh short retelling.
lessons.home: Write four timeline sentences; revise regular and irregular verbs.

lessons.title: Describe an interrupted event
lessons.outcome: Identify background and event details in a narrative and combine past continuous with past simple.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 3/4 listening details; complete 4/5 tense choices; produce two clear background/event sentences.
lessons.prior: Past simple; be forms; action-ing.
lessons.vocab: cargo = goods transported by ship; crew = people working on a ship; rescue = help out of danger; suddenly = unexpectedly and quickly.
lessons.model: Sam was checking the cargo when he heard an alarm. The crew were waiting while the officer was speaking.
lessons.ccq: Which action was already in progress: checking or heard? Checking.
lessons.lead: Use p. 65 picture to predict the setting and feeling; separate predictions from known facts.
lessons.controlled: Listen to U4-B twice for gist and four facts. Complete p. 77 past-continuous items 1-5.
lessons.guided: Draw a timeline for the model; use p. 78 practice to connect an ongoing action with an event.
lessons.task: Witness interview: ask What were you doing when...? and answer with one background action and one event. Swap roles twice.
lessons.check: p. 77 items 1-5; complete: While they ___ (play), it ___ (start) to rain.
lessons.answers: was reading; were not playing; Were you watching; were waiting; were not sleeping. were playing / started. U4-B: checking cargo; alarm; life jacket; crew meeting point.
lessons.exitq: Complete: I ___ (walk) when I ___ (hear) a noise.
lessons.exitkey: was walking; heard. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students use two past-simple verbs without showing background.
lessons.support: Use a long timeline bar for the ongoing action and a dot for the event.
lessons.extension: Create a sentence with two simultaneous ongoing actions using while.
lessons.nextstep: Compare a timeline and two sentence options; then elicit one new example.
lessons.home: Complete selected p. 78 items; prepare a short past-event example.

lessons.title: Retell The Wise Tailor
lessons.outcome: Identify a story’s problem, response and resolution and retell it using past language.
lessons.criteria: Answer 5/7 p. 70 items; order four events; retell with a clear problem and ending.
lessons.prior: Past simple/continuous and time markers.
lessons.vocab: tailor = person who makes or repairs clothes; thorn = sharp point on a plant; reward = something given for an action; gratitude = thankfulness.
lessons.model: While the bee was drinking honey, Tim noticed a thorn. He removed it, and the bee stopped troubling the village.
lessons.ccq: Did Tim help the bee or attack it with a stick? He helped it.
lessons.lead: Use p. 68 predictions. Ask learners to explain that predictions may change after reading.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 69 and answer p. 70 items 1-7 independently. Identify the evidence for one false statement.
lessons.guided: Order four events: bee arrives; Tim attracts it; thorn removed; reward used for flowers. Practise p. 72 vocabulary gaps.
lessons.task: Retell the story to a partner who asks one why/how question. Give a different possible ending and clearly label it your own idea.
lessons.check: p. 70 items 1-7; p. 72 five vocabulary gaps.
lessons.answers: F, F, F; B, C, B, C. Gaps: tailor, mayor, thorn, honey, reward. Gratitude means thankfulness; its antonym is ingratitude, not angry.
lessons.exitq: State the bee’s problem and how Tim solved it.
lessons.exitkey: A thorn was in its foot; Tim removed the thorn. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students confuse a prediction or invented ending with the text.
lessons.support: Use three labels: prediction / text fact / my ending.
lessons.extension: Explain a lesson from the story using a supporting event.
lessons.nextstep: Give one true event and one invented event to classify, then ask a new evidence question.
lessons.home: Plan a personal or invented event using p. 79 prompts; bring five notes for Thursday.

lessons.title: Write a memorable-event narrative
lessons.outcome: Write a coherent 100-150-word narrative with a setting, event sequence, ending and appropriate past tenses.
lessons.criteria: Include who/where/when; use three past-simple verbs and one past-continuous clause; include a clear ending in 100-150 words.
lessons.prior: Story structure; past tenses; sequence language.
lessons.vocab: setting = where/when a story happens; sequence = order of events; resolution = how the problem ends; memorable = easy to remember.
lessons.model: Last Thursday, I visited a workshop with my class. While we were watching a demonstration, the lights went out.
lessons.ccq: Which sentence gives the setting, and which gives the interruption? First; second.
lessons.lead: Use p. 74 house prompts for two quick past statements, then retrieve one story opener.
lessons.controlled: Correct three tense errors on the companion page; underline the setting and ending in the U4 model.
lessons.guided: Use p. 79 planning questions: who, where, when, events, feelings and ending. Rehearse to a partner before writing.
lessons.task: Write 100-150 words independently. Use the p. 80 checklist and U4 rubric; partner identifies one clear detail and one useful revision.
lessons.check: Edit: Yesterday I go. While we waited, the bus arrived (make waiting ongoing). Did you saw it?
lessons.answers: Yesterday I went. While we were waiting, the bus arrived. Did you see it?
lessons.exitq: Write one corrected background/event sentence and name one revision made to your paragraph.
lessons.exitkey: 1 accurate tense contrast + 1 specific revision supported by the draft. Assess the full narrative with U4 rubric.
lessons.barrier: Students spend too long planning and leave no time to draft.
lessons.support: Limit notes to five boxes; use timed planning and a word-count target.
lessons.extension: Add relevant sensory detail without exceeding 150 words.
lessons.nextstep: Use the most common tense or organisation problem for next week’s opening revision.
lessons.home: Submit the revised narrative with one sentence explaining what you improved.

inputs: U4-A | The car stopped | Sunday

Last Sunday, Ahmed was travelling with his sister when their car stopped. They called a mechanic and waited in a safe place. At the garage, the mechanic checked the car and found a faulty alternator. He explained the repair before starting. Ahmed asked about the cost and warranty. After the work, the mechanic tested the car. Ahmed felt relieved because he could continue his journey. He told his sister that asking clear questions had helped him understand the problem.
Questions: What happened? Who was with Ahmed? Which part was faulty? How did he feel after the repair?
Key: car stopped; sister; alternator; relieved. These are invented classroom details, not the original Salim-audio answers.
U4-B | An alarm on a ship | Tuesday

Sam was checking the cargo when he heard an alarm. He stopped his task and listened to the officer. The officer told the crew to follow the ship’s emergency procedure. Sam collected his life jacket and went to the crew meeting point. While the crew were waiting, the officer checked their names. Later, the team confirmed that everyone was accounted for. Sam felt calmer because he knew where to go and whom to listen to.
Questions: What was Sam doing? What did he hear? What did he collect? Where did he go?
Key: checking cargo; alarm; life jacket; crew meeting point. Do not infer the date, destination or crew number from the original book task.
card: Story structure cards

SETTING: who, where and when. BACKGROUND: action already in progress. EVENT: something happened. RESPONSE: what people did. ENDING: result or feeling. Ask learners to arrange their notes under these headings before drafting.
resources.model: Last Thursday, my class visited a training workshop in Salalah. I was excited because it was my first visit. At the beginning, the instructor introduced the equipment and explained the rules. While we were watching a demonstration, the lights suddenly went out. Everyone stopped and listened carefully. The instructor asked us to stay calm, and another teacher checked the situation. A few minutes later, the lights came back on. We continued the visit and asked many questions about the tools. Before we left, I thanked the instructor for explaining everything clearly. I felt proud because I had used English to ask a question. It was an experience I will remember.
rubric: Clear who/where/when setting
Logical event sequence and ending
Accurate past-simple verbs
Appropriate past-continuous background clause
100-150 words; clear linking and punctuation
resources.quick: 1. go -> past ___. 2. Correct: Did he went? 3. Complete: She ___ reading when I arrived. 4. The bee’s problem in The Wise Tailor was ___.
resources.quickkey: 1 went; 2 Did he go?; 3 was; 4 a thorn in its foot.
resources.feedback: Your story has a clear ending. Check the background action: use was/were + -ing. After did or didn’t, use the base verb.

units.name: Made in Oman
units.focus: Traditional products, boatbuilding, industry, materials, present passive and an Omani company presentation.

lessons.title: Describe traditional Omani products
lessons.outcome: Find key information about traditional Omani products and describe a material/source and a use.
lessons.criteria: Match 2/3 headings; answer 3/4 selected detail questions; independently give two accurate product facts.
lessons.prior: Common product names; simple present sentences.
lessons.vocab: resin = sticky substance from trees; pottery = objects made from clay; kiln = oven used to fire clay; sheath = cover that holds a blade.
lessons.model: This is Omani pottery. It is made from clay. It is used for decoration.
lessons.ccq: Does frankincense come from clay or tree resin? Tree resin.
lessons.lead: Show p. 83 product pictures. Learners name them and predict a material or use.
lessons.controlled: Skim p. 83; match the headings in p. 84 A. Compare only after an individual attempt.
lessons.guided: Answer p. 85 D1-2 and the two E comprehension questions. Underline the relevant text before discussing.
lessons.task: Craft-stall role-play: expert describes a product; visitor asks its material/source and use, chooses one and explains why. Swap roles.
lessons.check: p. 84 headings; p. 85 D and E comprehension questions.
lessons.answers: Headings A-3, B-1, C-2; 4 extra. D: B, B. E: e.g., burned for fragrance and used in perfumes; pots used for decoration, souvenirs, cooking or storage.
lessons.exitq: Name one traditional product, state its material/source and give a use.
lessons.exitkey: 1 accurate material/source point + 1 accurate use point. Target 2/2; reading scores recorded separately.
lessons.barrier: Students confuse a product, its material and its use.
lessons.support: Use product / material-source / use columns and a picture word bank.
lessons.extension: Compare two products with one similarity and one difference.
lessons.nextstep: Use a clay/resin sort, explain corrections, then hide the model and request a new sentence.
lessons.home: Write three product facts and revise resin, pottery, kiln and sheath.

lessons.title: Listen to a boatbuilding account
lessons.outcome: Identify boatbuilding details in a spoken account and summarise the main ideas.
lessons.criteria: Match 5/6 vocabulary definitions; retrieve 3/4 listening details; give a four-sentence summary.
lessons.prior: Traditional products; material and purpose language.
lessons.vocab: craftsman = skilled maker; maritime = related to the sea; voyage = long journey; heritage = traditions passed between generations.
lessons.model: A craftsman builds wooden boats. The boats connect maritime work with Omani heritage.
lessons.ccq: Is maritime related to the sea or farming? The sea.
lessons.lead: Use a boat picture and ask what materials and skills may be needed.
lessons.controlled: Complete p. 86 A vocabulary matching. Listen to U5-A once for main idea, then again for four details.
lessons.guided: Fill material / maker / use / heritage notes; compare and prepare a four-sentence summary using p. 88 structure.
lessons.task: Museum-guide pairs explain traditional boats to a visitor. Each speaker answers one question about skills or heritage.
lessons.check: p. 86 A1-6; U5-A questions. Distinguish century from voyage.
lessons.answers: craftsman; ports; maritime; century; heritage; voyages. Extra: flexible. Century = 100 years; voyage = journey. U5-A key: wood; craftsman; fishing/travel; preserve skills/heritage.
lessons.exitq: Define craftsman and give one purpose of traditional boats from the listening.
lessons.exitkey: Skilled maker; fishing/travel. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students copy isolated words without connecting ideas.
lessons.support: Use four labelled note boxes and sentence starters.
lessons.extension: Contrast traditional skills with one possible modern method; label opinions as opinions.
lessons.nextstep: Read a fresh short description; learners record two facts and turn them into connected sentences.
lessons.home: Complete a four- or five-sentence summary as on p. 88.

lessons.title: Read about industry in Oman
lessons.outcome: Identify paragraph ideas and classify products, utilities and facilities in an industry text.
lessons.criteria: Match 3/4 headings; classify 6/8 items; answer three factual questions using text evidence.
lessons.prior: Omani product vocabulary; reading for gist and detail.
lessons.vocab: industrial estate = area with industries; utility = supplied service such as electricity; facility = place/service supporting users; export = send goods to another country.
lessons.model: The text lists electricity as a utility, a bank as a facility, and furniture as a product.
lessons.ccq: Is a bank something the factory makes or a facility people use? A facility.
lessons.lead: Brainstorm what a group of factories needs: services, products and places for workers.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 90; complete p. 91 heading matches A-D and locate the date information.
lessons.guided: Sort roads, water, electricity, bank, clinic, furniture, paints and filters into the three p. 91 categories.
lessons.task: Design a simple industrial-estate plan with labelled utilities, facilities and products. Explain two choices using because.
lessons.check: p. 91 A; according to the 2024 text, when was Rusayl completed and when is Industry Day?
lessons.answers: A-2, B-1, C-5, D-4; 3 extra. Text dates: 1982 and 9 February. Utilities: roads/water/electricity; facilities: bank/clinic; products: furniture/paints/filters.
lessons.exitq: Classify electricity and furniture, then give one supporting explanation.
lessons.exitkey: Electricity: utility; furniture: product. 1 point for each correct classification; explanation confirms understanding.
lessons.barrier: Students confuse a product with a service.
lessons.support: Ask Is it made for sale? or Does it help the factory operate?
lessons.extension: Discuss the text’s housing restriction using a reason rather than an unsupported fact.
lessons.nextstep: Use two borderline examples and ask for a reason before assigning a category.
lessons.home: Use products, utilities and industrial estate in sentences, as on p. 92. Treat numerical claims as text information.

lessons.title: Describe production with the passive
lessons.outcome: Identify broad production information and form present-passive sentences about products.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 3/4 listening details; complete 4/5 passive forms; describe a product in three passive sentences.
lessons.prior: Materials vocabulary; is/are; past participles such as made and used.
lessons.vocab: mill = machine for grinding; kiln = high-temperature oven; raw material = input used to make a product; passive = sentence pattern focusing on the affected thing.
lessons.model: Cement is produced in a factory. Machines are used to process materials. Products are checked before delivery.
lessons.ccq: In Cement is produced, is cement doing the action or receiving it? Receiving it.
lessons.lead: Compare People make products with Products are made. Ask which word receives the focus.
lessons.controlled: Read U5-B twice; answer its four questions. Sort selected p. 95 words into natural materials and manufactured products.
lessons.guided: Use pp. 98-99 to complete five present-passive gaps; rewrite two present-tense active sentences.
lessons.task: Factory-guide role-play: explain three stages using is/are + past participle. Visitor asks what is made or checked. Swap.
lessons.check: p. 99 five gaps: cement/make; machines/use; factory/maintain; products/inspect; methods/apply.
lessons.answers: is made; are used; is maintained; are inspected; are applied. U5-B: factory; kiln; mill; checked/packed. p. 99 built example is past passive; use builds for present practice.
lessons.exitq: Complete: Pottery ___ (make) from clay. Products ___ (export).
lessons.exitkey: is made; are exported. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students omit be or use a base verb after it.
lessons.support: Use product / is-are / past participle cards; contrast one item and several items.
lessons.extension: Add a negative: These products are not made from plastic.
lessons.nextstep: Repair two passive errors, then give a new singular and plural prompt.
lessons.home: Use the U5 company fact card to prepare three presentation notes for Thursday; optional official-site research.

lessons.title: Present an Omani company
lessons.outcome: Present a short, sourced company profile with accurate product information and present-passive examples.
lessons.criteria: Give four sourced facts; use two appropriate passive sentences; answer one audience question clearly.
lessons.prior: Traditional/modern products; present passive; note-taking.
lessons.vocab: source = where information comes from; profile = short description; founded = started as an organisation; conductor = material/component that carries electrical current.
lessons.model: Oman Cables Industry was established in 1984. It makes electrical cables. Cables are used in power networks.
lessons.ccq: Should an unknown date be guessed or checked in a source? Checked.
lessons.lead: Distinguish a company fact from an opinion using the U5 company card.
lessons.controlled: Identify company name, founding date, product and use on the verified resource card. Underline the supporting source.
lessons.guided: Use pp. 96-97 prompts to plan introduction, products, materials/uses and a source line. Practise two passive sentences.
lessons.task: Give a 60-90-second profile to a small group; answer one question. Each learner submits a four-fact note card and two passive sentences for assessment.
lessons.check: Check the company name/date/product/use and correct: Cables is used. Products are make.
lessons.answers: Oman Cables Industry; 1984; electrical cables; power networks/infrastructure. Cables are used. Products are made. The historical was established is a model chunk, not present passive.
lessons.exitq: Write one sourced company fact and one accurate present-passive sentence.
lessons.exitkey: 1 verified fact + 1 accurate present passive. Assess the presentation separately with the U5 rubric.
lessons.barrier: Students read a copied paragraph instead of communicating from notes.
lessons.support: Limit cards to keywords; rehearse with a partner and point to the source.
lessons.extension: Compare this company’s product with one traditional product.
lessons.nextstep: Review the weakest area: source accuracy, passive form or answering a question.
lessons.home: Improve the profile after feedback; record the official source and access date.

inputs: U5-A | Traditional boats | Monday

Our guide describes traditional wooden boats. A craftsman needs patience, experience and careful measuring skills. Wood is shaped and joined to make the boat. These boats connect with fishing and travel in Oman’s maritime history. Visitors today can learn about the craft and the people who practise it. Preserving boatbuilding skills helps younger people understand this heritage. The guide asks us to notice the material, the maker and the purpose rather than memorising many dates.
Questions: What material is named? Who makes the boat? Give one use. Why preserve the skills?
Key: wood; craftsman; fishing/travel; to preserve heritage and understanding.
U5-B | A factory description | Wednesday

This classroom description follows materials through a factory. First, raw materials are prepared. A kiln is used during heating, and a mill is used for grinding. Machines help workers process the materials. The finished products are checked before they are packed. The guide explains that a process description can focus on the products: materials are prepared, machines are used, and products are checked. We record these passive forms in our notebooks.
Questions: Where is the process? Which machine is linked to heating? Which to grinding? What happens before packing?
Key: factory; kiln; mill; products are checked. This is a language model, not a technical manufacturing procedure.
card: Company fact card | Oman Cables Industry

Founded in 1984; manufactures electrical cables; supports power networks and infrastructure. Copper is identified as a cable material in its 2022 annual report. Sources: official Our Journey page and 2022 annual report; see the final reference page. Students may use this card offline or verify another company.
resources.model: Today I am introducing Oman Cables Industry. It was established in 1984. The company manufactures electrical cables. Cables are used in power networks and infrastructure. Copper is used in cable manufacture. My information comes from the company’s official website and annual report. This example shows how an Omani industrial product supports everyday services.
rubric: Four accurate, source-supported facts
Clear introduction, products and uses
Two suitable present-passive sentences
Clear speaking from notes
Relevant answer to one question and a named source
resources.quick: 1. Pottery is made from ___. 2. Resin comes from ___. 3. Complete: Products ___ exported. 4. A bank in an industrial estate is a product / facility.
resources.feedback: The product information is clear. Add the source to your note card. Practise one more present-passive sentence and answer without reading the whole paragraph.

units.name: Instructions
units.focus: Procedures, sequence markers, imperatives, present passive and a 100-150-word process paragraph.

lessons.title: Understand clear fire-safety instructions
lessons.outcome: Recognise instruction verbs and order the PASS words in a classroom language task.
lessons.criteria: Identify 4/4 PASS verbs; retrieve 3/4 listening points; produce three clear imperative sentences.
lessons.prior: Action verbs; workshop safety vocabulary.
lessons.vocab: imperative = command/instruction using a base verb; nozzle = outlet directing a spray; pin = removable locking piece; evacuate = leave for safety.
lessons.model: Open the book. Read the instructions. Do not guess. The PASS words are pull, aim, squeeze and sweep.
lessons.ccq: After Do not, do we use uses or use? Use.
lessons.lead: Use textbook pictures to identify equipment parts; discuss why instructions need a clear order.
lessons.controlled: Listen to U6-A and answer its four language questions. Order the four PASS verbs using p. 104.
lessons.guided: Use p. 113 rules and p. 114 A gaps; practise positive/negative instructions with ordinary classroom actions.
lessons.task: Pairs sequence word cards and explain the order. Give a new student three classroom instructions; partner follows using paper/book objects only.
lessons.check: p. 104 order; p. 114 A1-4; explain the form after do not.
lessons.answers: Pull, aim, squeeze, sweep. A: open; press; add/mix; turn. Use a base verb after do not. Live extinguisher operation belongs to trained staff and site procedures.
lessons.exitq: Write one affirmative classroom instruction and one negative instruction.
lessons.exitkey: 1 correct base-verb imperative + 1 correct do not + base verb sentence.
lessons.barrier: Students add to or an -s ending to imperatives.
lessons.support: Compare You open the book with Open the book; remove the subject, keep the base verb.
lessons.extension: Explain how first and finally help a listener.
lessons.nextstep: Correct two imperative errors and ask for an original classroom example.
lessons.home: Practise p. 114 language items. Use fire content as text analysis; no live equipment practice.

lessons.title: Sequence a planting procedure
lessons.outcome: Identify the order of a planting procedure and retell it with sequence words and imperatives.
lessons.criteria: Order 5/5 selected steps; answer 2/3 true/false items; give four instructions in a sensible sequence.
lessons.prior: Imperatives; first/next/then/finally; plant vocabulary.
lessons.vocab: seedling = young plant; compost = material added to improve soil; transfer = move to another place; harvest = collect a mature crop.
lessons.model: First, choose suitable seeds. Next, plant them in a tray. Then, prepare the soil. Finally, check that the instructions are in order.
lessons.ccq: Does finally normally mark the beginning or the ending? The ending.
lessons.lead: Use p. 105 pictures to predict the order of seed selection, planting and transfer.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 106 and complete B ordering and C true/false items. Mark the words that signal each stage.
lessons.guided: Convert the six headings into imperative sentences. Use first, next, then, after that and finally without changing the procedure.
lessons.task: Explain the planting sequence to a partner using shuffled cards. Listener restores the order and asks one clarification question.
lessons.check: p. 106 B in printed order; C1-3. Name the stage after seed planting.
lessons.answers: B: 3,5,2,4,1. C: T,F,F. After seed planting: prepare land/pot. Keep the transfer and harvest details tied to the text.
lessons.exitq: Order choose seeds / plant seeds / transfer seedlings, then write one imperative.
lessons.exitkey: Correct order as listed; any accurate planting imperative. 1 order point + 1 sentence point.
lessons.barrier: Learners add sequence words but leave the steps illogical.
lessons.support: Order picture/heading cards before adding linking words.
lessons.extension: Explain why one step must come before another using because.
lessons.nextstep: Give three new process cards; check order first, then the sentence form.
lessons.home: Write four to six steps from the text; complete the sequencing language on p. 111.

lessons.title: Explain how a house is built
lessons.outcome: Identify construction stages and describe a simple process using sequence markers and present passive.
lessons.criteria: Order 5/6 stages; retrieve 3/4 listening details; form four accurate present-passive sentences.
lessons.prior: Unit 5 passive; sequence words; construction tools.
lessons.vocab: foundation = supporting base; plaster = material used to coat walls; beam = supporting structural piece; stage = part of a process.
lessons.model: First, the foundations are laid. Next, the walls are built. The roof is added, and the walls are painted.
lessons.ccq: Are walls doing the building, or are people building them? People build them.
lessons.lead: Use p. 107 picture to name three parts of a house and predict which is built first.
lessons.controlled: Listen to U6-B twice. Order its six stages; compare with p. 108 vocabulary without assuming the two audio tasks are identical.
lessons.guided: Use p. 115 transformations and p. 116 negatives. Build a four-sentence process from the p. 117 word bank.
lessons.task: Builder/client explanation: describe a house process using passive sentences; client asks What happens next? Swap, then write the process.
lessons.check: p. 115 B1-4. Make negative: The tools are checked.
lessons.answers: The food is prepared. The classrooms are cleaned every day. New bridges are built. Vegetables are grown. The tools are not checked.
lessons.exitq: Complete: The walls ___ (build). The roof ___ (add).
lessons.exitkey: are built; is added. 1 point each; target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Students confuse imperative instructions with passive descriptions.
lessons.support: Contrast Build the wall with The wall is built and identify their purposes.
lessons.extension: Add a negative passive sentence and explain its meaning.
lessons.nextstep: Ask learners to label two imperatives/two passives, then create one of each.
lessons.home: Complete the short house-process paragraph on p. 117 and revise irregular participles.

lessons.title: Sequence and report a workshop response
lessons.outcome: Report an incident accurately and sequence a short account using clear instructions and connectors.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve 3/4 listening details; order four response events; deliver a clear location/problem/help message.
lessons.prior: Unit 3 incident language; Unit 4 past; sequence markers and imperatives.
lessons.vocab: first-aid kit = materials for initial care; bleeding = losing blood; reassure = help someone feel calmer; report = give information about an event.
lessons.model: First, Ali heard Hamad call. Next, he alerted the first aider. Then, he gave the location. Finally, he followed the trained person’s instructions.
lessons.ccq: Do we invent a treatment that the account did not mention? No.
lessons.lead: Read the short incident on p. 110 and identify who, where and what is known.
lessons.controlled: Use U6-C instead of unavailable audio; listen for the four stated events and put them in order.
lessons.guided: Separate the original p. 110 facts from the teacher-created continuation. Write four event sentences using sequence markers.
lessons.task: Reporter/receiver role-play: relay the incident; receiver repeats the place and problem. Then explain the four-event sequence using notes.
lessons.check: p. 110: Who is injured? Where? Who hears him? U6-C: who is called and what is reported?
lessons.answers: Hamad; carpentry workshop; Ali. Adapted continuation: trained first aider is called; location and bleeding problem are reported. Do not treat the script as the original audio key.
lessons.exitq: Write a two-step report using first and next, with one source-supported fact in each.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point per accurate event with an appropriate connector. Target 2/2.
lessons.barrier: Learners mix the textbook event with invented treatment advice.
lessons.support: Use separate Text facts and Adapted continuation boxes; practise reporting, not medical procedures.
lessons.extension: Give one concise checking question a receiver could ask.
lessons.nextstep: Read a new short incident and check that only stated details are reported.
lessons.home: Plan the Thursday chili-planting paragraph using p. 118 verbs and the Unit 6 model.

lessons.title: Write a clear process paragraph
lessons.outcome: Write a well-ordered 100-150-word process paragraph using imperatives and sequence markers.
lessons.criteria: Include purpose and at least five steps; use four sequence markers; write 100-150 words with consistent imperative form.
lessons.prior: Planting procedure, imperatives, sequencing and editing.
lessons.vocab: process = series of actions leading to a result; draft = first version; sequence marker = word showing order; checklist = points used to review work.
lessons.model: To grow chili plants, prepare the materials first. Next, choose suitable seeds and follow the seed-packet directions.
lessons.ccq: Should instructions keep changing between I planted and Plant? No; keep the chosen form consistent.
lessons.lead: Compare two versions of three steps; identify which is easier to follow and why.
lessons.controlled: Edit the three imperative/sequence errors on the companion page. Notice the structure of the U6 model.
lessons.guided: Use p. 118 to plan purpose, materials, ordered steps and closing. Check verbs and sequence before drafting.
lessons.task: Write 100-150 words independently. Partner follows the sequence on paper and checks missing steps; revise using the U6 rubric.
lessons.check: Edit: First, to prepare the pot. Next, plants the seeds. Finally, you watered it yesterday.
lessons.answers: First, prepare the pot. Next, plant the seeds. Finally, water it as directed. Accept other consistent, logical final instructions.
lessons.exitq: Write one improved instruction and explain which sequence or verb error you corrected.
lessons.exitkey: 1 accurate imperative + 1 specific explanation linked to the draft. Use the process rubric for the full paragraph.
lessons.barrier: Students write a list of disconnected commands without a clear purpose or order.
lessons.support: Provide purpose / materials / steps / final check boxes; use the model only for structure.
lessons.extension: Rewrite two steps in present passive to contrast process description with instructions.
lessons.nextstep: Review the portfolio and choose one personal target for the next course or revision lesson.
lessons.home: Submit the final process paragraph and a short reflection on one skill improved across Level 2.

inputs: U6-A | Instruction language | Sunday

Today we are reading about fire-safety instructions. The four PASS words are pull, aim, squeeze and sweep. The textbook links them with the pin, the base of a fire, the handle and a side-to-side movement. In this English lesson, we put words and pictures in order. Real extinguisher use requires appropriate training and authorisation. Everyone follows the site emergency plan and evacuation instructions.
Questions: What are the four words? What part is linked with pull? What action is linked with the handle? What plan must people follow?
Key: pull/aim/squeeze/sweep; pin; squeeze; site emergency plan. Use cards only.
U6-B | A house process | Tuesday

First, the house is planned. Next, the foundations are laid. The walls are built after the foundations. Then, the roof is added. After that, the inside walls are plastered. Finally, the house is painted and checked. This is a short overview. The words first, next, then, after that and finally help the listener follow the sequence.
Task: Order planning, foundations, walls, roof, plastering and painting. Identify two passive verbs.
Key: sequence as listed; e.g., are laid, are built, is added, are plastered, is painted.
U6-C | A teacher-created continuation | Wednesday

First, Ali heard Hamad calling for help in the carpentry workshop. Next, Ali alerted the trained first aider. Then, he clearly reported the location and said that Hamad’s arm was bleeding. Finally, Ali followed the first aider’s instructions while other learners stayed clear. The class later practised giving a short and accurate message.
Questions: Who called? Where? Who was alerted? What information was reported?
Key: Hamad; carpentry workshop; trained first aider; location and bleeding arm. This does not reproduce the original treatment audio.
card: Choosing language for a process

Instruction: Prepare the soil. Negative instruction: Do not skip the check. Passive description: The soil is prepared. Keep the chosen form consistent with the task. Actual planting conditions follow the seed packet and local growing guidance.
resources.modeltitle: Model: a process paragraph for chili plants
resources.model: To grow chili plants, prepare your materials and choose seeds suitable for your area. First, read the seed packet and collect a tray, suitable soil and a label. If the packet recommends soaking, soak the seeds as directed. Next, fill the tray with soil and plant the seeds at the recommended depth. Label the tray so that you can identify the variety. Then, water carefully according to the packet instructions and place the tray in a suitable position. Check the seedlings regularly as they grow. After that, prepare larger pots and move the seedlings when they are ready. Finally, continue caring for the plants and record the changes you observe.
rubric: Clear purpose and necessary materials
At least five logically ordered steps
Consistent imperative forms
Four appropriate sequence markers
100-150 words; readable paragraph and final check
resources.quick: 1. Correct: Please to open the book. 2. Negative: Use the phone. 3. Complete: The walls ___ built. 4. Which word signals the last step?
resources.quickkey: 1 Please open the book; 2 Do not use the phone; 3 are; 4 finally.
resources.feedback: The order is clear. Remove to from the imperative opening and check that each step begins with a base verb. Add a final check if the reader needs one.

units.name: Travel and Culture
units.focus: Travel reading/listening, comparisons, relative clauses, first conditional and 100-150-word source analysis.

lessons.title: Read travel advice and listen for details
lessons.outcome: Identify useful travel advice and support a recommendation with evidence from a text.
lessons.criteria: Answer 4/5 selected reading items; retrieve 3/4 listening details; recommend two actions with reasons
lessons.vocab: local = belonging to an area; cuisine = a style of cooking; souvenir = object kept as a reminder; culture = shared practices and ideas; ceremony = formal event.
lessons.model: The text recommends learning basic local words because this shows respect. It also suggests buying locally made souvenirs to support the local economy.
lessons.ccq: Does the text say you will definitely like every local dish? No. Is a souvenir a memory itself or an object reminding you of it? An object.
lessons.lead: Learners choose three things they would learn before visiting a new place; explain one choice.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 8 and complete MC1-5 across pp. 9-10. Underline the supporting words before comparing answers.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U1-A, a fictional celebration account. Identify the main purpose, then record occasion, place, activity and gift.
lessons.task: In pairs plan a respectful first visit to an unfamiliar place. Use two ideas from the reading and one sensible question for a local host.
lessons.check: Reading MC1-5, pp. 9-10. U1-A: occasion/place/activity/gift?
lessons.answers: MC: B,B,B,C,D. U1-A: graduation; family home; meal and speeches; notebook. This is a fictional personal account, not a claim about a whole culture.
lessons.exitq: State one recommendation from p. 8 and explain the reason the text gives.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: accurate recommendation. 1 point: linked text reason. Example: buy local souvenirs; support the local economy.
lessons.barrier: Learners give personal opinions when asked for text evidence.
lessons.support: Use two columns: The text says / I think. Require one underlined clue for a reading answer.
lessons.nextstep: Give a fresh statement and ask learners to label it text evidence or personal opinion.
lessons.home: Finish selected short answers on pp. 11-12; prepare two questions for a travel partner.
lessons.prior: Basic spoken English and familiar college/workplace experiences; diagnose in the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Describe people, places and journeys
lessons.outcome: Summarise a journey story and describe people or places with defining relative clauses.
lessons.criteria: Answer 4/5 story questions; complete 4/5 relative words; describe a person, thing and place clearly
lessons.vocab: anticipation = expectation of something ahead; boarding = getting onto a plane/ship; attire = clothes; companionship = being with others; forge = form or develop in forge a friendship.
lessons.model: Anna is the traveller who took the train. A boarding pass is a document that a passenger uses. An airport is a place where travellers wait.
lessons.ccq: Does who refer to a person or place? Person. In the story, does forged a friendship mean worked metal or formed a relationship? Formed a relationship.
lessons.lead: Predict why two strangers might speak at an airport. Retrieve passport, boarding pass and delay.
lessons.controlled: Read p. 15 and answer MC1-5 on pp. 16-17. Explain Anna's and Sarah's different travel choices.
lessons.guided: Complete p. 25 Part 1; combine a person, thing and place description from the story using who/which/that/where.
lessons.task: Create a three-sentence visitor guide to an invented station or airport. Include a helpful person, useful object and waiting place; partner checks clarity.
lessons.check: Story MC1-5; relative words p. 25 Part 1; explain forge in the story.
lessons.answers: Story: A,B,C,D,B. Relative words: where; which/that; where; who/that; which/that. Forge here means form/develop, not a metalworking furnace.
lessons.exitq: Join: A guide helps visitors. A guide knows the city. Then complete: This is the station ___ we meet.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: A guide who/that knows the city helps visitors, or equivalent. 1 point: where.
lessons.barrier: Learners use where before a verb that needs a subject, e.g. a city where is busy.
lessons.support: Compare a place which is busy with a place where we meet; identify the subject after where.
lessons.nextstep: Use a new place example and ask learners to choose which or where and explain why.
lessons.home: Complete selected p. 25 sentence combinations and draft a short p. 26 travel brochure.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Compare travel choices and check details
lessons.outcome: Compare travel choices using stated data and confirm journey details in an exchange.
lessons.criteria: Retrieve four journey details; form 4/5 comparison phrases; recommend one of three options using two data facts
lessons.vocab: single ticket = one-way ticket; return ticket = outward and return journey; platform = train boarding area; fare = ticket price; comparative = compares items; superlative = ranks within a group.
lessons.model: In our fictional table, the train is faster than the bus. The taxi is the fastest option, but it is the most expensive. Say cheaper than, not more cheaper.
lessons.ccq: Are these prices real travel prices? No, classroom examples. Does the fastest refer to the highest speed within the stated group? Yes.
lessons.lead: Compare bus/train/taxi using learners' own criteria, then distinguish opinion from a number in a table.
lessons.controlled: Complete the five comparison forms in the companion check using pp. 23-24 and the travel-options card.
lessons.guided: Listen twice to U1-B. Note destination, departure time, platform and fare. Practise checking a misunderstood number.
lessons.task: Travel desk role-play: recommend an option from the card based on time and price. Customer asks two questions; adviser uses two comparisons and one superlative.
lessons.check: Forms: cheap; fast; expensive; good; the ___ (fast) of three. U1-B four details? Table: cheapest and fastest options?
lessons.answers: cheaper; faster; more expensive; better; fastest. U1-B: Riverton; 10:15; platform 3; 12 rials. Table: bus cheapest (5), taxi fastest (30 minutes). All figures and destinations are fictional.
lessons.exitq: Use the options card to write one accurate comparative and one superlative sentence.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point each for correct form and correct data. Example: The train is cheaper than the taxi. The bus is the cheapest option.
lessons.barrier: Learners form a comparison correctly but reverse the quantities.
lessons.support: Draw arrows from each phrase to the supporting table cells.
lessons.nextstep: Give a new small table and check one independent evidence-based comparison.
lessons.home: Write the p. 23 comparison blog using the fictional card or verified facts; identify opinions as opinions.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add a reason or a new example, then explain it to a partner.

lessons.title: Explain travel plans and possible results
lessons.outcome: Explain a travel plan and an alternative using accurate first-conditional sentences.
lessons.criteria: Choose 4/5 conditional forms; complete three possible-result sentences; agree on a plan and a backup with reasons
lessons.vocab: condition = situation needed for a result; result = what follows; reservation = advance booking; delay = later-than-planned event; alternative = another choice.
lessons.model: If it rains, we will visit the museum. If the museum is closed, we will go to the market. If + present simple; will + base verb.
lessons.ccq: Are we describing a possible future or a past event? Possible future. Do we normally put will directly after if in this pattern? No.
lessons.lead: Show rain, a closed museum and a missed bus as fictional planning problems; learners suggest alternatives.
lessons.controlled: Complete p. 27 MC1-5; underline the condition and circle the result clause.
lessons.guided: Complete p. 28 Part 2 items 1-5; partners explain why the verb belongs in that form.
lessons.task: Plan a one-day visit using the classroom travel card. Include two activities, two conditional backup plans and one relative-clause description.
lessons.check: p. 27 MC1-5; p. 28 Part 2 items 1-5. Correct: If it will rain, we will stay inside.

The article “Providing guidance and support through online learning” appeared in The Star on 23 February 2021. The textbook reproduces it as an example of an authentic source. It describes support for online learning during the pandemic and includes positive comments from parents. These comments suggest that the families quoted valued the school’s help.

lessons.criteria: Answer 4/4 text true-false items; match four modal meanings; explain three safety messages with text support
lessons.vocab: procedure = agreed way to do something; cluttered = untidy and crowded with items; inspect = examine carefully; hazard = potential source of harm; PPE = personal protective equipment.

lessons.ccq: Does mustn't mean not necessary? No, it means prohibited. Does PPE remove every risk? No.
lessons.lead: Learners predict the six headings from pp. 35-36 using the title and workshop pictures.
lessons.controlled: Read pp. 35-36; answer the four T/F items and correct false statements with a text clue.
lessons.guided: Sort the companion modal sentences as requirement, prohibition or advice; compare the text's six safety themes.
