inputs: U2-A | Reporting a concern | Monday

Learner: There is a box blocking the walkway by the training-room door. Shall we put up a sign? Supervisor: Thank you for reporting it. A sign alone would leave the route blocked. Learner: Who can arrange for the box to be moved safely? Supervisor: I will contact the responsible staff and arrange safe clearance. Please follow our college procedure while we deal with it.
Questions: Where is the problem? What blocks the route? What is the first suggestion? Why is it insufficient? Who arranges clearance?
Key: walkway by training-room door; a box; put up a sign; route would remain blocked; supervisor, with responsible staff. Classroom language scenario.
card: COMPARISON CARD | GLOVES AND GOGGLES

Shared purpose: selected personal protective equipment can reduce exposure to particular hazards. Both need suitable selection, fit, inspection and training. Difference: gloves protect hands; goggles protect eyes. Glove material and goggle type depend on the task and hazards. Ordinary gloves do not protect against every chemical or electrical hazard; ordinary goggles are not universal protection for welding. Follow college-approved training and procedures.
extra: 1 Introduction: name both items and state the comparison focus. 2 Similarities: shared protective purpose; correct selection and use. 3 Differences: body part and task-specific type/material. 4 Conclusion: summarise why selection depends on the task. Useful links: both, similarly, whereas, in contrast, however. Explain a point instead of merely listing it.
resources.model:
Gloves and goggles are two types of personal protective equipment used in many training and work settings. Both can help reduce exposure to particular hazards, but they protect different body parts. A useful comparison considers their shared purpose and their task-specific differences.

Both items need to be selected for the hazards involved. They should fit the user and be checked before use. Training is also necessary because equipment offers limited protection when it is unsuitable or used incorrectly. Neither item replaces appropriate workplace procedures.

The main difference is the part of the body protected. Gloves protect the hands, whereas goggles protect the eyes. Selection also involves different features. Glove material must suit the task and exposure, while the type of goggles must suit the eye hazard. For example, ordinary gloves cannot be assumed to protect against every chemical or electrical hazard. Similarly, ordinary goggles are not suitable for every kind of welding work.

In conclusion, gloves and goggles share a protective purpose, but they are not interchangeable. Learners should follow the college’s approved procedures and ask the trainer which equipment is required for a particular activity.
rubric: Introduction names both items and a clear comparison focus
Balanced explanation of shared features
Accurate differences linked to task-specific selection
Clear comparison links and accurate sentence forms
Organised 150-250-word essay with a justified conclusion
resources.quick: 1. Gloves protect hands, ___ goggles protect eyes (whereas/because). 2. Correct: Gloves which protects hands. 3. If the label is unclear, I ___ (ask) the trainer. 4. Does mustn’t mean optional?
resources.quickkey: 1 whereas; 2 Gloves protect hands / gloves which protect hands, within a complete sentence; 3 will ask; 4 no, prohibited.
resources.feedback: You explain the shared purpose well. Add one specific difference and show why the correct type depends on the task.

inputs: U3-A | Photovoltaic energy | Monday

Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight into electricity. Panels contain these cells and can be installed where they receive suitable sunlight. Their output depends on the available light, so it can change during cloudy weather. Panels do not generate solar electricity at night. Systems may use the electricity grid or suitable storage to help meet demand when solar output is low. Different installations need different designs.
Questions: What technology is described? What is the energy input? What is the output? Give one availability limitation.
Key: photovoltaic cells/panels; sunlight; electricity; cloudy conditions can reduce output / no solar generation at night. Adapted explanation, not the official audio.
card: PROJECT COMPARISON | FICTIONAL UNITS

Project A: cost 10, output 4. Project B: cost 15, output 6. Project C: cost 20, output 8. Compare only these stated measures: A has the lowest cost; C has the highest output; B costs more than A. All three have the same output-to-cost ratio. The table does not establish which project is safest or most sustainable.
extra:
Climate check: greenhouse gases slow heat loss to space. Human activities, especially burning fossil fuels, increase greenhouse gases and drive current warming. The ozone hole is not the main cause of global warming.
Fictional writing case: a training centre puts mixed waste in one bin; labels are unclear and new students have not been shown the sorting system. Propose two explained actions, name responsible people and explain how improvement could be checked. Do not invent survey results.
resources.modeltitle: Model | Problem-solution essay | Pack target: 150-250 words
resources.model:
In a fictional training centre, recyclable materials are often mixed with other rubbish. Unclear labels and limited instruction make it difficult for students to sort their waste. This can prevent suitable materials from reaching the correct collection stream. Two practical changes could address the problem.

First, the centre could provide clearly labelled collection points. Staff should check which materials the local collection service accepts before choosing the labels. Pictures and short examples would help users understand each category. If the labels match the collection rules, students will have clearer guidance about where to put their waste.

Second, tutors could give a short demonstration to each new class. Learners could sort picture cards and explain their choices before using the collection points. A member of staff could record common sorting mistakes before and after the demonstration to check whether understanding improves.

These actions combine clearer information with practical language support. The centre would need to assign responsibility for the labels, demonstrations and follow-up checks. Starting with one area would allow staff to improve the system before extending it. Clear responsibilities and regular review would make the plan more feasible.
rubric: Clear problem with relevant causes and effects
Two specific solutions explained logically
Feasible responsibilities and a way to check improvement
Accurate condition-result links and coherent paragraphs
Complete 150-250-word response to the defined classroom case

resources.feedback: Your actions address the problem. Explain who will carry out each action and how the centre could check improvement.

units.name: Interpreting Data
units.focus: Essay structure and types; tables, pie/bar/line charts; comparisons, trends and accurate data descriptions.

lessons.title: Organise essays and choose the right purpose
lessons.outcome: Distinguish comparison, problem-solution and data-description purposes and organise a clear paragraph.
lessons.criteria: Match three tasks to their writing purpose; identify four structural elements; produce a focused paragraph with support
lessons.vocab: genre = kind of text with a purpose; thesis = whole-essay focus; topic sentence = paragraph focus; evidence = supporting facts/examples; overview = summary of main patterns.
lessons.model: A comparison essay explains similarities and differences. A problem-solution essay explains a problem and responses. A data report describes the figures shown, without inventing causes.
lessons.ccq: Is I think these sales rose because advertising improved supported by a chart alone? No. Does a topic sentence control one paragraph or the whole essay? One paragraph.
lessons.lead: Display three prompts: compare gloves/goggles; solve mixed waste; describe a chart. Learners identify the purpose of each.
lessons.controlled: Use pp. 86-93 to label thesis, topic sentence, evidence and conclusion in the companion examples.
lessons.guided: Review pp. 95-97 and 109-112. Sort connectors as similarity, contrast, result or sequence; plan one short paragraph.
lessons.task: Write a five-sentence paragraph for one prompt and explain its purpose to a partner. Partner checks every sentence supports the topic.
lessons.check: Match prompts: similarities/differences; problem/actions; numerical patterns. Functions: whole-essay focus; paragraph focus; example; final synthesis. Connectors: similarly/however/therefore/first.
lessons.answers: Comparison; problem-solution; data description. Thesis; topic sentence; supporting evidence; conclusion. Similarity; contrast; result; sequence.
lessons.exitq: Write a focused topic sentence for a data report and explain what information it must identify.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point for a suitable sentence naming the chart topic; 1 point for identifying relevant time period/unit/category information.
lessons.barrier: Learners give opinions when the task asks for a factual description.
lessons.support: Mark statements as shown by data or not shown; keep invented causes out of the report.
lessons.nextstep: Use two sample statements and ask which the displayed data supports.
lessons.home: Review the comparison and problem-solution essays from earlier units; improve one topic sentence in each.

lessons.title: Read tables and pie-chart proportions
lessons.outcome: Read units and categories accurately and compare quantities and proportions.
lessons.criteria: Answer four table questions; retrieve four pie-chart values; describe two comparisons without changing the units
lessons.vocab: category = group of items; proportion = part of a whole; percentage = part out of 100; native speaker = person who learned a language from early childhood; unit = measurement used.
lessons.model: In the textbook practice table, English has 1.5 billion learners. In the water-use chart, the garden accounts for 35%. A percentage is not the same as a number of people.
lessons.ccq: Is 1.5 billion the same as 1.5 million? No, it is 1,500 million. Does the pie chart show change over time? No.
lessons.lead: Identify title, labels and units in the p. 121 table and p. 122 pie chart before reading values.
lessons.controlled: Answer the four companion questions about p. 121. Treat the table as practice data, as its note states.
lessons.guided: Read p. 122; answer questions 1-4 and check that all five percentages total 100. Separate factual questions from the opinion questions 5-6.
lessons.task: In pairs present two table comparisons and two pie-chart comparisons. Partner checks each number and unit against the source.
lessons.check: p. 121: most learners? most native speakers? fewest learners? English-speaking countries shown? p. 122: bathroom, laundry, kitchen, garden?
lessons.answers: English; Chinese; Japanese; 101 countries. Water: bathroom 26%, laundry 15%, kitchen 5%, garden 35%; toilet 19%; total 100%. Laundry exceeds kitchen by 10 percentage points, not 10%.
lessons.exitq: State the largest water-use category and calculate the percentage-point difference between laundry and kitchen.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: garden, 35%. 1 point: 10 percentage points (15 minus 5).
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse percentages, percentage points and absolute quantities.
lessons.support: Write the unit beside every value; subtract labelled percentages to show percentage-point difference.
lessons.nextstep: Give a new 40% versus 25% comparison and check the 15-percentage-point difference.
lessons.home: Write four factual sentences from pp. 121-122; attempt the p. 123 bar-chart reading exercise as consolidation.

lessons.title: Describe trends and changes precisely
lessons.outcome: Describe change over time with accurate verbs, numbers and from/to/by/at.
lessons.criteria: Classify 4/5 trend patterns; complete 4/5 trend-language items; describe a short time series with accurate values
lessons.vocab: trend = general pattern over time; rise = increase; fall = decrease; remain stable = stay the same; peak = highest point; fluctuate = rise and fall.
lessons.model: In the classroom series, production rose from 20 to 70, an increase of 50. It remained at 70, then fell to 20. Use past tense for completed periods.
lessons.ccq: If a value rises from 20 to 70, does it rise by 70? No, by 50. Does remained at describe change? No, stability.
lessons.lead: Draw rising, falling, flat and changing lines; learners match them to ordinary words before technical labels.
lessons.controlled: Use the trend cards in the input bank to label five patterns; review p. 124 past/present verb groups.
lessons.guided: Complete the five companion trend-language items; describe the p. 117 first example while avoiding units not shown in that graph.
lessons.task: Information gap: A describes four classroom values (20,70,70,20); B draws the pattern and checks the numbers. Swap roles using 10,20,15,25.
lessons.answers: Rise; fall; remain stable; fluctuate; rise then rise more sharply. Forms: from; to; by; at; rose. Past: increase-increased, grow-grew, go up-went up.
lessons.exitq: Describe the change from 30 to 45 using both from/to and by.
lessons.exitkey: 1 point: rose/increased from 30 to 45. 1 point: rose/increased by 15.
lessons.barrier: Learners confuse the final value with the amount of change.
lessons.support: Label start, end and difference, then attach from, to and by.
lessons.nextstep: Use a fall from 50 to 35 and check fell by 15 in a new sentence.
lessons.home: Complete p. 127 gap-fill items 1-7; use the source chart for values and avoid unsupported forecasts.
lessons.prior: Familiar words from the unit and the previous lesson; check during the lead-in.
lessons.extension: Add one further numerical comparison, show the calculation and check units. Use only figures shown in the source.

lessons.title: Select key features and plan a report
lessons.outcome: Select an overview and supporting figures for an accurate comparison of two data series.
lessons.criteria: Answer 5/6 chart checks; identify two main patterns; plan a report with four supporting numbers and correct units
lessons.vocab: series = related values across time; overview = main patterns without every detail; steadily = at a fairly regular rate; dramatically = by a large amount; gap = difference between values.
lessons.model: The textbook chart shows spending in country X from 2011 to 2015, in millions of dollars. Both series rose overall. Computer spending increased steadily; smartphone spending rose later.
lessons.ccq: Does the chart show numbers of devices or money spent? Money spent. Can the chart prove what happened in 2016? No.
lessons.lead: Read the p. 128 title, axes and legend. Learners state the topic, period, categories and units before interpreting patterns.
lessons.controlled: Answer p. 126 MC1-6 using p. 125/128 chart. Check the two series at the beginning and end.

lessons.title: Write an accurate data description
lessons.outcome: Write an organised report describing the main features of a bar chart with accurate data and comparisons.
lessons.criteria: Correct four data-language errors; plan an overview and grouped details; write 150-200 words with accurate figures and units
lessons.vocab: accuracy = correctness; evidence = data supporting a statement; expenditure = money spent; overall = considering the full pattern; unsupported = not justified by the data.
lessons.model: Computer expenditure rose from 30 million dollars to 50 million. Smartphone expenditure remained at 10 million until 2013, before rising to 45 million in 2015.
lessons.ccq: May we invent reasons for the increase? No. Does 150-200 words come from a printed instruction on p. 128? No; it is this pack's practice target.

lessons.guided: Review the plan and rubric: introduction, overview, two detail groups and selected comparisons. Check all numerical claims before drafting.

card: CHART REFERENCE | TEXTBOOK p. 128

The chart describes money spent on computers and smartphones in country X, 2011-2015. Values are in millions of dollars. Use the table and chart below to check every sentence. These are textbook practice figures, not current market statistics.
extra:
Textbook p. 122 water use: garden 35%, bathroom 26%, toilet 19%, laundry 15%, kitchen 5%. Total 100%. Laundry exceeds kitchen by 10 percentage points.
Textbook p. 121 language table: most learners = English; most native speakers = Chinese; fewest learners = Japanese; English shown in 101 countries. The book labels these practice data.
Classroom trend series: 20, 70, 70, 20 = rise, remain stable, fall. Alternative: 10, 20, 15, 25 = fluctuate. From 20 to 70 is an increase of 50. Describe only what the data supports.
resources.modeltitle: Model | Data description | Pack target: 150-200 words
resources.model:
The bar chart compares spending on computers and smartphones in country X between 2011 and 2015. The figures are measured in millions of dollars.

Overall, spending on both categories increased during the period. Computer spending rose steadily, while smartphone spending remained unchanged at first and then grew substantially. Computers accounted for more spending in every year shown.

In 2011, computer spending stood at 30 million dollars. It increased by 5 million each year, reaching 50 million in 2015. This was an overall rise of 20 million.

Smartphone spending remained at 10 million dollars from 2011 to 2013. It then climbed to 30 million in 2014 and reached 45 million in the final year. Its total increase was 35 million, larger than the increase for computers. By 2015, the difference between the two categories was only 5 million dollars, compared with 20 million in 2011. Combined spending rose from 40 million to 95 million over the period. The chart does not explain the reasons for these changes.
rubric: Accurate topic, period, categories and units
Clear overview of both main patterns
Correct figures with at least two useful comparisons
Logical grouping and accurate trend language
150-200 words describing data without invented causes or forecasts

resources.quickkey: 1 50 million dollars; 2 35 million dollars; 3 95 million dollars; 4 from / to / of (or rose by 20).
resources.feedback: Your overview is clear. Check every number against the chart and distinguish the final value from the amount of change.
